IN MIRATIONS ON THE PSALMS II
[ARDANT WISHES OF THE BALANIZED TO SEE THE SANCTUARY AGAIN]

SERMON TO THE PEOPLE 1 [v.1.3]. Ordinarily, our soul desires to rejoice with you in the word of God and to keep you in him, because it is our help and our health. Hear from me what God gives and rejoice with me in him, in his word, charity and truth. We have undertaken the exposition of a psalm suitable to your desire. This psalm begins with a holy desire, and the singer says: As the deer desires the spring of water, so does my soul desire you, O God! Who says this? If we want, we. What do you look for outside of yourself who this is, when it is in your power to be what you seek? However, it is not a man, but a body, and the body of Christ is the Church. Nor is this desire found in all those who enter the Church. However, those who tasted the sweetness of the Lord and perceived the content of the song, do not think that they are alone, but believe that such bushes are planted in the field of the Lord, which occupies the whole earth, and that of any Christian unity is this voice: As the deer desires the spring of water, so does my soul desire you, O God! Therefore, it is correctly understood that this voice is the PSALMUS

1 [v.1.3]. Olim est ut desiderat anima nostra in verbo Dei gaudere vobiscum, et in illo vos salutare, qui est nostrum adiutorium et salutare. The title of the psalm is as follows: A Psalm for the end, to the sons of Korah, of understanding. In the titles of other psalms we also find the sons of Korah; I remember having already discussed this and having indicated to you the meaning of this name. Therefore, now this title must be commemorated in such a way that beforehand it does not predispose us to not speak more than what we have already said, so that from now on we will not say more, since where we spoke of this name not everyone was there. Korah was a man who actually existed and had children, who were called sons of Korah. However, let us scrutinize the secret of the mystery so that the name makes us aware of the arcane that it contains. It is a great mystery that Christians call themselves children of Korah. Where does it come from that they are called children of Korah? To be called children of the husband, children of Christ. For Christians are called children of the husband (in the Gospel). Why is he called Christ Korah? Because Korah means skull or skull. The waters are taken from very far away. Verumtamen, fratres, videtur mihi etiam in Baptismate fidelibus nondum esse satiatum tale desiderium: sed fortassis, si norunt ubi peregrinentur, et quo eis transeundum sit, etiam ardentius inflammantur. 2. why Christ appears to belong to the skull. Wasn't the crucifixion carried out at the place of the skull? It certainly took place there. Then the children of the bridegroom, the children of his passion, the children redeemed with his blood, the children of his cross who carry on their foreheads what the enemies fixed in the place of the skull, are called children of Korah. This psalm is sung to them so that they understand. Then we stretch our understanding so that, if it is sung to us, we understand. What are we to understand? In what sense is this psalm sung? I dare say that the invisible things of Him, since the creation of the world, are visible through those that have been made. Hey, brothers, perceive my longing, make common cause with me in this longing; We love together, together we are inflamed by this thirst, let us run together to the source of this understanding. Let us desire the fountain like the deer, but not the fountain that those who are to be baptized for the remission of sins long for. We who have already been baptized let us desire that source of which another psalm says: In you is the source of life. This source is light, because in your light we will see the light. Therefore, if it is a source and is light, it is rightly also understanding, because it satisfies the soul eager for knowledge; and everyone who understands is illuminated by a certain non-corporeal, non-material, not external, but internal light. Therefore, brothers, there is a certain inner light, which those who do not understand lack. Hence the Apostle already speaks, pleading with those who desire this source of life, and from which they perceive something, saying to them: No longer walk like cavideatur. Nonne iam occurrit in loco Calvariae crucifixus? (Mt 27,33). Occurrit omnino. Intellectu itaque excitemur; et si nobis cantatur, intelligamus. Quid intellecturi sumus? in quem intellectum psalmus iste cantatur? Audeo dicere: invisibilia enim eius a creature mundi per ea quae facta sunt intellecta conspiciuntur (Rom 1,20). Eia, fratres, aviditatem meam capite, desiderium hoc mecum communicate: simul amemus, simul in hac siti exardescamus, simul ad fontem intelligendi curramus.

But what if the deer desires the spring of water to bathe, since we do not know whether it desires it to drink or bathe? Let us hear what follows and not question: My soul thirsts for the living God. And why this? To contemplate—he says—the delight of the Lord. When will I go and see the face of the Lord? 6 [v.4]. Meanwhile, while I consider, while I run, while I am on the path before I come and appear in your presence, my tears are my bread day and night, when it is said to me every day: Where is your God? My tears, he says, are not bitterness to me, but bread. These tears were delightful to me, because, being thirsty for this fountain, as I could not yet drink, I ate my tears more eagerly. He did not say: These tears served as a drink for me, nor does it seem that He desired them like the spring of waters, but, as that thirst persisted for which I burn, for which I am drawn to the fountain of waters, when I was held, my tears became bread. And certainly, eating his tears, he undoubtedly feels the need for the fountain more. My tears are my bread day and night. Men eat this food called bread during the day, and at night they sleep. The bread of tears is eaten day and night, whether you take the entire time of life as day and night, whether you understand the prosperity of this life by day, and its adversity by night. In the prosperous things of this world and in the adverse ones, I, he says, shed the tears of my desire, I do not lose the avidity of my desire, and, when it adapts to the world, it becomes an evil for me before I present myself before God. Is it not temporary, fickle, passing? Isn't it more disappointing than attractive? So why shouldn't these things be my bread of tears? Let us not forget that, when the happiness of this world smiles upon us, while we live in body, we walk towards God and that I am continually told: Where is your God? If a pagan tells me this, can't I also ask him: Where is your God? When he shows me his god with his finger, directing his finger towards a stone, and says to me: Here is my god, I can continue asking him: Where is your God? If I laugh at the stone and the person who showed it to me is ashamed, he turns his eyes away from it; He looks at the sky, and perhaps points his finger at the sun, and again says: There is my god. Again I can say to him: Where is your God? He finds something to show to the eyes of the flesh, but I can't show him anything; not because I have nothing to show him, but because he lacks eyes to whom I can show my God. He was able to show his god, the sun, to the eyes of my body. To whose eyes will I show the Creator of the sun? 7. However, hearing every day: Where is your God?, and nourished daily with my tears, I thought day and night what I heard: Where is your God?; and I also sought my God, so that, if possible, I might not only believe in him, but also see him. I contemplate the breadth of the vast sea; I am stunned, I admire myself, I look for the Artificer. I look at the sky, and I see the beauty of the stars; I contemplate the splendor of the sun exercising the lordship of the day and I observe the moon tempering the darkness of the night. These things are wonderful; They are worthy of being praised or admired; They are not earthly, but celestial. Yet the longing of my thirst is not there. I admire these things, I praise them, but I thirst for the One who made them. I go inside myself and probe who it is that I investigate these things, and I see that I have body and soul; one, whom I must rule; another, by which I must rule; The body must obey, the soul command. I distinguish that the soul is much better than the body, and I see that the very investigator of these things is not the body, but the soul; and yet all these things that I examined I know that I examined through the body. I praised the land, I knew it through its eyes. I praised the sea, I knew it by its eyes. I praised the sky, the stars, the sun and the moon, I knew them through their eyes. The eyes are members of flesh; They are the windows of the mind, inside is the one who sees through them; When thought is lacking, they are open in vain. My God, who made these things that I see with my eyes, should not be sought by them. Let the soul also look at something for itself, and see if there is anything that it does not perceive with the eyes, such as colors and light; nor by the ears, like singing and noise; nor through the nostrils, like the fragrance of odors; nor for the palate and the meum? I consider terram: facta est terra. Est magna pulchritudo terrarum; sed habet artificem. Magna miracula sunt seminum atque gignentium; sed habent ista omnia creatorem. Ostendo magnitudeinem circumfusi maris, stupeo, miror; artificem quaero: caelum suspicio et pulchritudinem siderum; admire splendorem solis exserendo diei sufficientem, lunam nocturnal tenebras consolantem. Mira sunt haec, laudanda sunt haec, vel etiam stupenda sunt haec; ñeque enim terrena, sed iam caelestia sunt haec. Nondum ibi stat sitis mea: haec miror, haec laudo; sed eum qui fecit haec, site. Redeo ad meipsum, et quis sim etiam ipse qui talia quaero, perscruror: invenio me habere corpus et animam; unum quod regam, aliud quo regar; corpus I will serve, animam imperare.

Discerno animam melius esse aliquid quam corpus, ipsumque inquisitorem talium rerum non corpus, sed animam video: et tamen haec omnia quae collustravi, per corpus ea me collustrasse cognosco. Terram laudabam, oculis cognoveram; mare laudabam, oculis cognoveram; caelum, sidera, solem lunamque laudabam, oculis cognoveram. Oculi membra sunt carnis, fenestrae sunt mentís: interior est qui per has videt; quando cogitatione aliqua absens est, frustrates patent. Deus meus qui fecit haec, quae oculis video, non istis oculis est inquirendus. Aliquid etiam per seipsum animus ipse conspiciat: utrum sit aliquid quod non per oculos sentiam, quasi colors et luzm; non per aures, quasi cantum et sonum; non per nares, quasi odorum suavitatem; non per palatum et linguam, quasi sa-

tongue, like flavor; nor for the whole body, such as hard and soft, cold and hot, rough and smooth; but if there is something you see inside. What does it mean to see inside? Let him see what is not color, nor sound, nor smell, nor taste, nor heat, nor cold, nor hardness, nor softness. Tell me what color wisdom is. When we think of justice and rejoice in its beauty internally in thought, what do we hear? What kind of steam rises to our nose? What do you like in your mouth? What do we touch with our hands that delights us? And yet, she is within, and she is beautiful, and she is praised, and she is seen; In fact, if our eyes are dark, the soul rejoices in its own light. What did Tobias see when, blind, he advised his son, who saw, with words of eternal life? Then there is something that the soul, lady, rector, inhabitant of the body, sees; but it does not perceive it through the eyes, nor through the ear, nor through the nose, nor through taste, nor through the touch of the body, but through itself, and better through itself than through its servant. It also happens, without a doubt, that the soul sees itself, and to see itself it does not ask the bodily eyes for help; Furthermore, to see itself in itself, to know itself together with itself, it withdraws towards itself, separating itself from all the senses of the body as from objects that disturb and impede. But is God something similar to what the soul is? God certainly can only be seen by the soul, but he cannot be seen as the soul is seen. The soul seeks something that is God, so those who say to it: Where is your God, do not mock it? Look for a reality

immutable reality, a most perfect substance. The soul is not such, because it progresses and decays, knows and ignores, remembers and forgets, once it wants and another time it does not want. This change does not occur in God. If I said that God is changeable, those who say, Where is your God, would mock me? 8 [v. 5]. I look for my God among visible and corporeal things, and I do not find Him. I look for its substance in myself, as if it were something equal to me, and I don't find it. I feel that it is something that is above the soul. To perceive Him I meditated on these things and poured out my soul within me. When will my soul perceive what is sought above it if not when it turns on itself? If it remained inactive, it would only see itself, and when it saw itself it would not see its God. Say now, my mockers: Where is your God? Talk. While I cannot see, as long as I am not taken away, I feed myself day and night with my tears. Still say: Where is your God? I look for my God in everything corporeal, whether terrestrial or celestial, and I do not find Him; I search my soul for its substance, and I do not find it; I gave myself to the search for my God, and for the things that have been made I desired to see the invisible things of my God. I poured out my soul upon myself, and there is no one left for me to perceive but my God. Above my soul is the house of my God; He lives there, from there he looks at me, from there he created me, from there he governs me, from there he looks at me, he encourages me, he calls me, he directs me, he guides me and he leads me. 9.

porem; non per totum corpus, quasi duritiem et mollitiem, rigorem atque fervorem, asperitatem lenitatemque pertractem; sed uttum sit aliquid intus quod videam. Quid est, intus videoam. Quod ñeque color sit, ñeque sonus, ñeque odor, ñeque sapor, ñeque calor, aut frigus, aut duritia, aut mollitudo. Dicatur ergo mihi, quem colorem habeat sapientia. Cum cogitamus iustitiam, eiusque intus in ipsa cogitatione pulchritudine fruimur, quid sonat ad aures? quid tanquam vaporeum surgit ad nares? quid ori infertur, quid manu tractatur et delectat? Et intus est, et pulchra est, et laudatur, et videtur: et si in tenebris sunt oculi isti, animus illius luz perfruítur. Quid est íllud quod Tobias videbat, quando vídenti filio caecus consilium vitae ibat? (Tob 4.2). Est ergo aliquid quod animus ipse corporis dominator, rector, habitator videt; quod non per oculos corporis sentit, non per aures, non per nares, non per palatum, non per corporis tactum, sed per seipsum: et utique melius quod per seipsum, quam quod per servum suum. Est prorsus; seipsum enim per seipsum videt, et animus ipse ut norit se, videt se. Nec utique ut videat se, corporalium oculorum quaerit auxilium: imo vero ab ómnibus corporis sensibus, tanquam impedientibus et perstrepentibus abstrahit se ad se, ut videat se in se, ut noverit se apud se. Sed numquid aliquid tale Deus ipsius est, qualis est animus? Non quidem videri Deus nisi animo potest, nec tamen ita ut animus videri potest. Aliquid enim quaerit animus iste quod Deus est, de quo illi non insultent qui dicunt: Ubi est Deus tuus? Aliquam quaerit incommutabilem veritatem, sine defectu substantiam. Non est talis ipse animus: deficit, proficit; novit, ignorat;

Quaerens ergo Deum meum in rebus visibilibus et corporalibus, et non inveniens; quaerens eius substantiam in meipso, quasi sit aliquid qualis ego sum, ñeque hoc inveniens; aliquid super animam esse sentio Deum meum. Ergo, ut eum tangerem, Haec meditatus sum, et effudi super me animam meam. Quando anima mea contingeret quod super animam meam quaeritur, nisi anima mea super seipsam effunderetur? Si enim in seipsa remaneret, nihil aliud quam se videret: et cum se videret, non utique Deum suum videret. Dicant iam insultatores mei, Ubi est Deus tuus? dicant: ego quamdiu non video, quamdiu differor, manduco die ac nocte lacrymas meas. Dicant illi adhuc, Ubi est Deus tuus? quaero ego Deum meum in omni corpore, sive terrestri, sive caelesti, et non invenio: quaero substantiam eius in anima mea, et non invenio: meditatus sum tamen inquisitionem Dei mei, et per ea quae facta sunt, invisibilia Dei mei cupiens intellecta conspicere (Rom 1:20), efjudi super me animam meam; et non iam restat quem tangam, nisi Deum meum. Ibi enim domus Dei mei, super animam meam: ibi habitat, inde me prospicit, inde me creavit, inde me gubernat, inde mihi consult, inde me excitat, inde me vocat, inde me dirigit, inde me ducit, inde me perducit. 9. He also has a tabernacle on earth. His tent or tabernacle on earth is his Church, still a pilgrim. But here it must be sought, because in the tabernacle is the way that leads to the house. When I poured out my soul on myself to see my God, why did I do this? For I must enter the place of the tabernacle. For outside the place of the tabernacle I will wander seeking my God. I will enter the place of the marvelous tabernacle to the house of God. I will enter the place of the tabernacle, the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God. Well, I already admire many things in the tabernacle. Here are how many things I contemplate in it. The tabernacle of God on earth is faithful men. In them I admire the obedience of their members, because sin does not reign in them obeying their desires; nor do they lend their members to sin as instruments of iniquity, but offer themselves to the living God in good works; I also observe that the members are under the dominion of the soul to serve God; I also contemplate the soul that obeys God by ordering the works of its actions, restraining concupiscence, abandoning ignorance and offering to endure all tribulations and annoyances, devoting itself above all to justice and charity. I contemplate these virtues in my soul, but I still find myself a pilgrim in the place of the tabernacle. I put all these things aside, and, although the tabernacle is wonderful, I am filled with amazement when I arrive at the house of God. He says of this house in another psalm when proposing the laborious and difficult question of why many times on earth things go well for the wicked, and evil.

the good ones, and answers: I took it upon myself to know him, but it is a great job for me until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand the last moments. There, in the sanctuary of God, in the house of God, is the fountain of understanding. There he understood the end times and resolved the question of the happiness of the wicked and the suffering of the righteous. How did you solve it? Seeing that, when the bad are tolerated here, they are reserved for eternal punishments, and, when the good suffer, they are trained to obtain the inheritance on the last day. He knew this in the sanctuary of God, he understood it in the last moments. Going up to the tabernacle, he came to the house of God. However, while he was contemplating the parts of the tabernacle, he was led to the house of God, carried away by a certain sweetness and I don't know what hidden inner delight, as if in the house of God some organ was playing sweetly that seduced him. Walking, then, through the tabernacle, upon hearing a certain interior sound, he was carried away by the sweetness, and, following what sounded, abstracted from all noise of flesh and blood, he arrived at the house of God. And he remembers his path and direction in such a way that, as if we were saying to him: In this land you were captured by the tabernacle; So, how did you get to the secret of the house of God? Answer: By the voices of joy and praise of the music of the one who celebrates a festival. When men celebrate their worldly festivals on earth, they have the custom of placing some musical instruments in front of the house, or of adjusting flute players, or of providing any kind of music that flatters and incites sensuality. When we hear this and those of us who pass by ask what is happening, we are told: It commemorates a

in terra tabernaculum. Tabernaculum eius in terra, Ecclesia eius est adhuc peregrina. Sed hic quaerendus est, quia in tabernacle invenitur via, per quam venitur ad domum. Etenim cum effunderem super me animam meam, ad attingendum Deum meum, quare hoc feci? Quoniam ingrediar in locum tabernaculi. Nam extra locum tabernaculi errabo quaerens Deum meum. Quoniam ingrediar in locum tabernaculi admirabilis, usque ad domum Dei. In locum tabernaculi ingrediar, admirabilis tabernaculi, usque ad domum Dei. Iam enim fine admirer in tabernacle. Ecce quanta admire in tabernacle! Tabernaculum enim Dei in terra, homines sunt fideles: admire in eis ipsorum membrorum obsequium; quia non in eis regnat peccatum ad obediendum desideriis eius, nec exhibitant membra sua arma iniquitatis peccato, sed exhibitant Deo vivo in bonis operibus: animae servienti Deo membra corporalia militare admiror (Ib. 6,12.13). Respicio et ipsam animam obedientem Deo, distribuentem opera actus sui, frenantem cupiditates, pellentem ignorantiam, extendentem se ad omnia áspera et dura toleranda, iustitiam et charitatem impendentem caeteris. Mirror et these virtutes in anima: sed adhuc in loco tabernaculi ambulo. Transeo et haec: et quamvis admirable sit tabernaculum, stupeo cum pervenio usque ad domum Dei. De qua domo dicit in alio psalmo, cum proposuisset sibi quamdam duram et difficilem quaestionem, quare in hac terra plerumque bene est malis, et male est bonis, et ait: Suscepi cognoscere, hoc labor est ante me, doñee introeam. in sanctuarium Dei,

et intelligam in new (Ps 72,16,17). Ibi est enim fons intellectus, in sanctuario Dei, in domo Dei. Ibi ¡ntellexit iste in novissima, et solvit quaestionem de congratulate iniquorum, et labore iustorum. How did I solve it? Quia malí cum hic differuntur, ad poenas sine fine servantur; et boni cum hic laborant, exercentur, ut in fine haereditatem consequantur. Et hoc ille in sanctuario Dei cognovit, intellexit in novissima. Ascendens tabernaculum, petvenit ad domum Dei. Tamen dum miratur membra tabernaculi, ita perductus est ad domum Dei, quamdam dulcedinem sequendo, interiorem nescio quam et oceultam voluptatem, tanquam de domo Dei sonaret suaviter aliquod organum: et cum ille ambularet in tabernacle, audio quodam interiore rang, ductus dulcedine, sequens quod sonabat, abstrahens se ab omni strepitu carnis et sanguinis, pervenit usque ad domum Dei. Nam viam suam et ductum suum sic ipse commemorat, quasi diceremus ei, Miraris tabernaculum in hac terra; quomodo pervenisti ad secretum domus Dei? In voce, inquit, exsultationis et confessionis, soni jestivitatem celebrantis. Festa cum hic homines celebrant suae quoque luxuriae, consuetudinem habent constituere organa ante domos suas, aut will put symphoniacos, vel quaeque music ad luxuriam servientia et illicientia. Et ubi audita fuerint haec, quid dicimus qui transimus? Quid hic agitur? And respond nobis, aliqua esse festa. Ñatalitia, inquit, celebrant, nuptiae hic sunt; ut non videoantur inepta illa

party; a birth is celebrated; there is a wedding And we are told this so that those songs do not seem inappropriate to us, but rather that the magnificence of the festival is excused in favor of grace. In the house of God, the festival is eternal, something transitory and passing is not celebrated there. The choir of angels celebrates eternal celebration before the presence of God with incessant joy. The holiday does not begin or end there. When the world does not make noise, the ears of the heart perceive, coming from that eternal and perpetual festivity, something lilting and sweet. The sound of that festival captivates the ear of him who walks in this tabernacle and considers the wonders of God in the redemption of the faithful; and likewise drags the deer to the fountain of waters. 10 [v.6.7]. But, brothers, since, while we live in the body, we make a pilgrimage towards God, and the corruptible body aggravates the soul, and the earthly abode depresses the spirit that thinks of many things, although in any case, walking with desire, with the darkness already vanished, we strive to obtain something from that house of God, nevertheless, while we reach this sound (of the sweetness of the house), due to a certain burden of our weakness, we fall back into the usual and we We slide into the ordinary and as there we find the reason for joy, so the cause for groaning is not lacking here. In fact, this deer, feeding day and night with its tears, being drawn by desire to the spring of waters, that is, to the internal sweetness of God, pours out its soul upon itself in order to obtain what is above it, and, walking in the place of the admirable tabernacle until it reaches the abode of God, is attracted by the song, sed excusetur festivitate luxuria. In domo Dei festivitas sempiterna est. Non enim aliquid ibi celebratur et transit. Festum sempiternum, chorus Angelorum: vultus praesens Dei, laetitia sine defectu. Dies hic festus ita est, ut nec aperiatur initio, nec fine claudatur. De illa aeterna et perpetua festivitate sonat nescio quid canorum et dulce auribus cordis: sed si non perstrepat mundus. Ambulanti in hoc tabernacle et miracula Dei in redemptionem fidelium considerati, mulcet aurem sonus festivitatis illius, et rapit cervum ad fontes aquarum. 10 [v.6.7].

Sed quia, fratres, quamdiu sumus in corpore hoc, peregrinamur a Domino (2 Cor 5,6), et corpus quod corrumpitur aggravat animam, et deprimit terrena inhabitatio sensummula cogitantem (Sap 9,15): etsi utcumque nebulis diffugatis ambulando per desiderium, ad hunc sonum pervenerimus interdum, ut aliquid of illa domo Dei nitendo capiamus; onere tamen quodam infirmitatis nostrae ad consueta recidimus, et ad sólita ista dilabimur. Et quomodo ibi inveneramus unde gauderemus, sic hic non deerit quod gemamus. Etenim cervus iste manducans die ac nocte lacrymas suas, raptus desiderio ad fontes aquarum, intetiorem scilicet dulcedinem Dei, effundens super se animam suam, ut tangeret quod est super animam suam, ambulans in locum tabernaculi admirabilis, usque ad domum Dei, et ductus interioris et intelligibilis soni iucunditate, ut omnia exteriora contemneret, et in interiora rapperetur; adhuc

pleasure of interior and intelligible sound, so that it despises all external things and is carried away by internal things. Yet he is still a man, he still groans in this world, he still carries his fragile flesh, he is still in danger among the stumbling blocks of this century. Now he looks towards himself, and, realizing that he comes from there (from seeing the ineffable sweetnesses), he says to himself, being placed among the bitternesses, which he compares with those things that he entered to see and that after seeing he left: Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Behold, we are happy because of a certain inner sweetness; You see that we were already able to contemplate something immutable with the gaze of the mind, although it was just barely and hastily. Why do you still trouble me? Why are you still sad? You no longer doubt your God, you now have something to say to those who shout: Where is your God? Since you have come to know something immutable, why do you still trouble me? Wait on God. And as if his soul answered him in silence (he tells him): Why do I trouble you if it is not because I am not yet there where the sweetness is found from which I was momentarily and as if in passing taken away? Do I now drink from that fountain without any fear? Should I no longer fear any stumbles? Am I already sure of all the lusts, as if they were tamed and defeated? Does not the devil, my enemy, lie in wait against me? Doesn't it daily lay insidious snares for me? Do you not want me to be troubled, finding myself in the world and still far from the house of my God? He waits in God, responds to his soul, which is itself disturbed and which seems to account for its disturbance due to the evils of which this world abounds. Meanwhile live in hope. For "the hope of what is seen is not hope; if we hope for what we do not see, we wait patiently." tamen homo est, adhuc hic gemit, adhuc carnem fragilem portat, adhuc inter scandala huius mundi periclitatur. Respexit ergo ad se, tanquam inde veniens, et ait sibi constituto Inter has tristitias, et comparans haec illis ad quae videnda ingressus est, et post quae visa egressus est: Quare, inquit, tristis es, anima mea, et quare conturbas me? Ecce iam quadam interiore dulcedine laetati sumus, ecce acie mentís aliquid incommutabile, etsi perstrictim et raptim, perspicere potuimus: quare adhuc conturbas me, quare adhuc tristis es? Non enim dubitas de Deo tuo. Non enim non est quod tibídicas, contra illos qui dictunt: Ubi est Deus tuus?

Iam aliquid incommutabile persensi, quare adhuc conturbas me? Spera in Deum. Et quasi responderet illi anima eius in silentio, Quare conturbo te, nisi quia nondum sum ibi, ubi est dulce illud, quo sic rapta sum quasi per transitum? Numquid iam bibo de fonte illo, nihil metuens? iam nullum scandalum pertimesco? iam de cupiditatibus omnibus tanquam edomitis victisque secura sum? Nonne adversus me diabolus vigilat hostis meus? nonne Iaqueos mihi quotidie deceptionis intendit? Non vis ut conturbem te posita in saeculo, et peregrina adhuc a domo Dei mei? Sed, Spera in Deum respondert conturbanti se animae suae, et quasi rationem reddenti perturbationis suae, propter mala quibus abundat hic mundus.

11. Wait on God. Why do I tell you wait? Because I will confess to him. What do you have to confess? Health of my face (is) my God. My health cannot come from me. This I will say, this I will confess: Health of my face (is) my God. Therefore, being afraid about the things that he knew in any way, worried, he returned to examine them again so that the enemy would not sneak in. That is why it does not yet say: I am completely safe. In fact, having the firstfruits of the spirit (however), we groan within ourselves waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body. We will have perfect health when we find ourselves living endlessly in the house of God and eternally praising Him to whom it was said: Blessed are those who dwell in your house and praise you forever and ever. This has not yet come, because the health that is promised has not yet been given to us; That is why I confess to my God in hope and say to Him: Health of my face (is) my God. By hope we have been saved, and the hope of what is seen is not hope. Persevere, then, in hope so that you arrive; Persevere until health comes. Hear your God, who speaks to you within you: Wait in the Lord, work with strength and let your heart be strengthened, and wait in the Lord, for whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. Then why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Wait on God, because I will confess to him. This is my confession: Health of my face (is) my God. 12. My soul is troubled within me. Are you disturbed

in God? In me it is disturbed. It is restored in the immutable, it is disturbed in the changeable. I know that God's justice persists, I do not know that mine persists. Well, the Apostle terrifies me when he says: He who thinks he is standing, let him not fall. Then, since I do not possess firmness nor trust in myself, my soul is troubled within me. Don't you want to be disturbed? Let not your soul rest in yourself and say: To you, Lord, I lift up my soul. Hear this very thing more clearly. Trust not in yourself, but in God. Because, if you trust yourself, your soul is troubled within you, because it has not yet found how to be sure of you. Therefore, since my soul is troubled within me, what is missing if not humility so that the soul does not presume on itself? All that remains for her is to make herself completely small, all that remains for her is to humble herself so that she deserves to be exalted. Do not attribute anything to yourself so that what is useful to you may be conferred on you by God. Then since my soul is troubled within me and pride is the cause of this disturbance, therefore I remembered you, O Lord, from the land of Jordan and from the little mountain of Herman. From where did I remember you? From the small mountain and from the land of Jordan. Perhaps from baptism, where the remission of sins occurs. In fact, only he who confesses to be a sinner runs to the remission of sins, and no one confesses to being a sinner except by humbling himself before God. Then from the land of Jordan I remembered you and from the little mountain. Not from the great mountain, so that you may make a small mountain into a great mountain, for he who exalts himself will be humbled and he who is humbled.

Interim inhabits in spe. Spes enim quae videtur, non est spes: si autem quod non videmus speramus, per patientiam exspectamus (Rom 8,24,25). 11. Spera in Deum. Quare Spera? Quoniam confitebor illi. Quid ei confiteberis? Salutare vultus mei, Deus meus. To me mihi salus esse non potest; hoc dicam, hoc confitebor: Salutare vultus mei, Deus meus. Hoc nondum est, quia nondum est salus quae promittitur: sed confiteor Deo meo in spe, et dico illi, Salus vultus mei, Deus meus. Audi ipsum Deum tuum de interiore tibi loquentem: Sustine Dominum, viriliter age, et comfortetur cor tuum, et sustine Dominum (Ps 26,14); quoniam qui perseveraverit usque in jinem, hic salvus erit (Mt 10,22, et 24,13). Quare ergo tristis es, anima mea, et quare conturbas me? Spera in Deum, quoniam confitebor illi. Haec est confessio mea, Salutare vultus mei, Deus meus. 12. Ad meipsum anima mea turbata est. We can speak to men, we can see them in the exercise of their limbs and hear them in conversation; but who penetrates his thoughts, who sees his heart? If man is an abyss, how does an abyss call another abyss? Does man call upon another man? But does it invoke him in the style as God is invoked? No. Invoke means to call towards oneself. It is said of a man who invokes death; that is, he lives in such a way that he calls death to himself. There is no one who prays for death; but, living badly, men call for death. An abyss calls to another abyss, a man to another man. This is how wisdom is learned, this is how faith is understood, calling one abyss to another abyss. You all also know who is advancing, who longs for the celestial city, who knows their pilgrimage, who is on the road, who anchored hope like an anchor in the desire for that most solid land. You also know that this class of men, this good seed, this wheat of Christ, groans among the tares; and this until the time of harvest arrives, that is, until the end of the world, as witnessed by the Truth, which is not mistaken. Groaning, then, among the tares, that is, among evil men, among the deceitful and seducers, whether agitated by anger or poisoned by snares; seeing that he is mingled with them throughout the world as in the same field, receiving the same rain, buffeted equally by the wind, nourished together with them in adversity and having at one with them these common gifts of God granted equally to the good and the evil by Him who makes the sun rise on the good and the evil and who rains on the just and the unjust; Seeing the lineage of Abraham, the holy race, how many things in common it now has with the evil ones, from whom at some time it must be separated, since they are born the same, the same condition of the human race falls into their lot, since they carry mortal bodies in the same way, they still enjoy the light, the sources, the fruits, the prosperity and adversities of the cem in omnibus Psalmis vel psallentem vel gementem, vel laetantem in spe, vel suspirantem in re, notissimam iam et familiarissimam habere debenmus, tanquam nostram. Non ergo diu est immorandum, ut insinuemus vobis quis loquatur: sit unusquisque in Christi corpore, et loquetur hic. 2 [v. l].

Nostis autem omnes qui proficiunt, et qui caelesti illi civitati ingemiscunt, qui peregrinationem suam norunt, qui viam tenent, qui in desiderio terrae illius stabilissimae spem tanquam ancoram praefixerunt: nostis ergo quia hoc genus hominum, hoc semen bonum, hoc frumentum Christi inter zizania gemit; et hoc doñee veniat tempus messis, id est usque in finem saeculi, sicut exponit quae non fallitur veritas (Mt 13:18). Gemens ergo inter zizania, id est inter malo homines, inter delosos et seductores, aut ira turbulentos, aut insidiis venenatos; circumspiciens simul cum illis esse se tanquam in uno agro per totum mundum, unam pluviam excipete, pariter perflari, pariterque secum inter adversa nutriri, habere simul ista communia dona Dei, malis bonisque concessa communiter ab illo qui facit solem suum oriri super bonds et malo, et pluit super iustos et iniustos (Ib. 5,45): videns ergo semen Abrahae, semen sanctum, quanta cum malis a quibus quandoque separandum est nunc habeat communia, aequaliter nasci, eamdem conditionem
An exile's desire to see the sanctuary

century; whether from famine of abundance, from peace of war, from health or from plague; Seeing, finally, how many things in common he has with the wicked, with whom, however, on the other hand, he has nothing to do, he bursts out with these words: Judge me, O God!, and separate my cause from unholy people. Judge me, he says, oh God! I do not fear your judgment, because I know your mercy. Judge me, O God, and separate my cause from unholy people. Now, while I am on this pilgrimage, you have not yet established my own place, for I live together with the tares until the time of harvest. You have not yet separated my rain, you have not yet separated my light; separates at least my cause. There is a difference between the one who believes in you and the one who doesn't believe in you. Weakness is equal, but consciousness is unequal; The suffering is the same, but the desire is different. The desire of the wicked will perish. We should doubt the desire of the just if it did not come from an incontrovertible promise. The term of our desire is the Promising One himself. He will give himself who gave himself. He will give himself, immortal, to the immortals, because he gave himself mortal to mortals. Judge me, O God, and separate my cause from unholy people. Deliver me from the perverse and deceitful man. This is the same as that of unholy people. Of man, of a certain kind of men, because there will be two kinds of men, and among these, "one will be taken and the other left." 3 [v. 2]. And, as there is a need to endure with patience until the time of harvest, a certain division can be called undivided, for it is mixed, and therefore is not yet found sepageneris humani sortiri, pariter mortalia ferré corpora, simul uti luz, fontibus, fructibus, prosperitatibus atque adversitatibus saeculi, sive fame, sive abundantia, sive, sive bello, sive salute, sive plague; videns quanta habeat communia cum malis, cum quibus tamen non habet causam communem, erumpit in hanc vocem: ludica me, Deus, et disceme causam meam de gente non sancta. ludica, inquit, me, Deus: non timeo iudicium tuum, quia novi misericordiam tuam. Ludica me, Deus, et discerne causam meam de gente non sancta.

Nunc interim in hac peregrinatione nondum discernís locum meum, quia simul cum zizaniis vivo usque ad tempus messis; nondum discernís pluviam meam, nondum discernís luzem meam: discerne causam meam. Distet inter eum qui in te credit, et eum qui in te non credit. Par infirmitas est, sed dispar conscientia: par labor, sed dispar desiderium. Desiderium impiorum peribit: de desiderio autem iustorum, nisi certus esset pollicitator, dubitare debenremus. Finís desiderii nostri, ipse promissor. Seipsum dabit, quia seipsum dedit: seipsum dabit immortalibus immortalem, quia seipsum dedit mortalibus mortalem. Ludica me, Deus, et disceme causam meam de gente non sancta. Ab homine iniquo et doloso erue me: hoc est, de gente non sancta. Ab homine, a quodam genere hominum, quia quidam homo et quidam homo, et in his duobus unus assumetur, et unus relinquetur (Ib. 24,40). 3 [v.2]. Et quoniam patientia opus est ferendi usque ad messem, quamdam, si dici potest, indiscretam discretionem; simul enim sunt, et ideo discrete nondum sunt; zizania autem zizania sunt, et frumenta fru-
Ennarrations on the Psalms

rada, although the tares are already tares and the wheat is already wheat, and, as for this, they are already separated; And since strength is necessary for this, we must obtain it from Him who commands us to be strong, because, if He who said: Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved does not make us strong, we will not be what is demanded. So that the soul does not weaken by assuming strength as its own, add next: Well, you, my God, are my strength, why did you reject me and why do I walk sad when the enemy oppresses me? Now he investigates the cause of his sadness, saying: Why am I sad when the enemy afflicts me? I am sad, because the enemy afflicts me with daily temptations, inspiring me with the idea that I love what I fear for no reason; And as the soul struggles against both things, if it does not fall, at least it staggers, and sadness takes over and it says to God: Why? God asks, and you will hear why. In the psalm he investigates the reason for his sadness, saying: Why did you reject me and why am I sad? I heard it from the mouth of Isaiah: The spirit proceeds from me and I made every breath; Because of his sin I grieved him a little and turned my face away from him; and he was sad, and so he goes sad on his way. What you wanted to know: Why did you reject me? Why am I sad? You heard it: Because of sin. The reason for your sadness is sin, let the reason for your joy be justice. You want to sin and you don't want to suffer. It would be little to you to be unjust if you had not wanted Him to be so, for whom you do not want to be avenged. Listen to another more excellent word in another psalm: It is good for me that you have humbled me so that I may learn your 'justices. I learned, proud, my iniquities; I will learn, humiliated, mint sunt, et ideo discrete iam sunt; quia ergo fortitudine opus est, imploring ab illo qui iussit ut fortes simus, et nisi fortes ipse fecerit, non erimus quod iussit, ab illo qui dixit, Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, bic salvus erit (Ib. 10,22, et 24,13); ne sibi ipsa anima arrogando fortitudinem debilitetur, continuo adiungit: Quia tu es, Deus meus, fortitudo mea; utquid me repulisti, et utquid tristis incedo, dum affligit me inimicus? Causam quaerit tristitiae suae. Quare, inquit, tristis incedo, dum affligit me inimicus?

Tristis ambulo, inimicus affligit me quotidianis tentationibus, immittens vel quod male amemus, vel quod male timeamus: et contra utrumque pugnans anima, etsi non Capta, tamen periclitans, contrahitur tristitia, et dicit Deo, Utquid? Quaerat ergo ab ipso, et audit utquid. Quaerit enim in Psalmo causam tristitiae suae, they say: Utquid me repulisti, et utquid tristis incedo? Audiat ex Isaia, succurrat illí lectio, quae moda recitata est: Spiritus, inquit, a me prodiet, et omnem flatum ego feci: propter peccatum modicum quid contristavi illum, et averti faciem meam ab illo; et contristcttus est, et abiit tristis in viis suis (Is 57,16,17). Quid ergo quaerebas, Utquid me repulisti, et utquid tristis incedo? Audisti: propter peccatum. Causa tristitiae tuae peccatum est, causa laetitiae tuae iustitia sit. Peccare volebas, et laborare nolebas; ut parum tibi esset quod esses iniustus, nisi et eum iniustum voluisses, a quo in te vindican noluisses. Réspice vocem meliorem in allio psalmo:
An exile's desire to see the sanctuary

your justices. Why do I walk sadly when the enemy afflicts me? You complain about the enemy; No doubt he afflicts you, but you are to blame, since you lodged him in your house. Now it is in your hand to act. Choose this advice: admit the King into your house and expel the tyrant from it. 4 [v. 3]. To do this, what do you say, what do you pray, what do you request? Take care. Ask for what you hear, ask when you hear, for this voice belongs to all of us: Send your light and your truth; They led me and took me to your holy mountain and your dwellings. Your light and your truth are two names, but one same thing. For what is the light of God but the truth of God? Or what is the truth of God but his light? And both things are one Christ. I am the light of the world; Whoever believes in me does not walk in darkness. I am the way, the truth and the life. He is the light, He is the truth. Then come and free us by now separating our cause from unholy people. Take us from the hands of "the wicked and lying man"; separate the wheat from the tares now. Because He will send His angels at the time of harvest to collect all the scandals from His kingdom and send them to the unquenchable fire and gather His wheat into the barn. Send your light and your truth, because they led us and took us to their holy mountain and their dwellings. We have the earnest money; Let's wait for the prize. His holy mountain is his holy Church. It is that mountain that, according to Daniel's vision, grew from the small stone and annihilated all the earthly kingdoms, and it became so immense that it occupied the entire face of the earth. From this mountain he affirms that Bonum est mihi quod humiliasti me, ut discam iustificationes tuas (Ps 118,71). Didiceram elatus iniquitates meas, discam humiliatus iustificationes tuas. Utquid tristis incedo, dum affligit me inimicus? Initially you will want; revera affligit, sed tu ei locum dedisti. Et nunc habes quod agas: choose consilium, regem admitte, tyrannum exelude. 4 [v.3]. Sed ut hoc faciat, quid dicit, quid supplicat, quid orat attende. Ora quod audis, ora cum audis; omnium nostrum sit ist vox: Emitte luzm tuam et veritatem tuam; ipsa me deduxerunt et perduxerunt in montem sanctum tuum, et in tabernacle, tua. Quia ipsa lux tua et veritas tua: haec nomina duo, res una. Quid enim aliud lux Dei, nisi veritas Dei? aut quid veritas Dei, nisi lux Dei? Et hoc utrumque unus Christus. Ego sum lux mundi: qui credit in me, non ambulabit in tenebris (lo 8,12).

Ego sum via, veritas et vita (Ib. 14,6). Ipse lux, ipse veritas. Veniat ergo, et eruat nos, discernens moda causam nostram a gente non sancta; eruat ab homine iniquo et doloso: separet frumentum a zizaniis: quia ipse mittet Angelos suos messis tempore, ut colligant de regno eius omnia scandala, et mittant in ignem ardentem, frumentum autem eius congregent in horreum (Mt 13,41.43). Emittat luzem suam et veritatem suam; quia ipsa iam nos deduxerunt et perduxerunt in montem sanctum eius et in tabernacula eius. Pignus habemus, praemium speramus. Sanctus mons eius, sancta Ecclesia eius. Mons ille est, qui crevit ex minimum lapide, secundum visionem Danielis, confringens regna terrarum; et in tantum excrescens, ut impleret universam faciem terrae
