The symbols of the things that are in the sacraments are realities in the perfection of eternal life. When we have passed to that rest, dear brothers, we will not fear there any enemy, any tempter, any envious person, any kind of fire or water, for there there will be perpetual rest. It's called rest for stillness. If you say it is heat, it truly is; If you say it is refreshment, it certainly is. If you misunderstand the word "refreshment", that is, if you understand it by cooling, then we will become numb there. We will not become numb there, but will rest. We will not burn there because it is called heat, but we will be inflamed in spirit. Observe this heat in another psalm: There is no one who escapes its heat. What does the Apostle also say? fervent in spirit. Then we have gone through fire and water. And you led us to rest. 18 [v.13]. See that he did not stop talking not only about rest, but not about the desirable fire itself, for he says: I will enter your house with burnt offerings. What is the holocaust? The sacrifice in which everything is burned, but with divine fire. The sacrifice or offering that is completely burned is called a holocaust. The portions of the sacrifices are one thing, and the burnt offering another. When everything burns and everything is consumed by fire in Sacramentis, hoc in tentationibus huius saeculi: anguish timoris accessit prima, vice ignis; post ablato timore, metuendum est ne congratulations mundana corrumpat. Cum autem te ignis crepare non fecerit, et in aquam non merseris, sed enataveris; per discipline! Transís ad requiem, et transiens per ignem et aquam educeris in refigerium. Quarum enim rerum signa sunt in Sacramentis, ipsae res sunt in illa perfectione vitae aeternae. Iam cum transierimus ad illud refrigerium, fratres charissimi, nullum ibi timebimus inimicum, nullum tentatorem, nullum invidum, nullum ignem, nullam aquam; perpetuum ibi refrigerium erit. Refrigerium propter quietem dicitur. Nam si dicas, Calor est, verum est: si dicas, Refrigerium, verum est. Si enim refrigerium male accipias, quasi torpescimus ibi.

Non autem torpescimus ibi, sed requiescimus: nec quia calor dicitur, aestuabimus ibi, sed fervebimus spiritu. Attende ipsum calorem in alio psalmo: Nec est qui se abscondat a calore eius (Ps 18,7). Quid dicit et Apostolus? Spiritu fervent (Rom 12,11). Ergo, Transivimus per ignem et aquam: Et eduxisti nos in refrigerium. 18 [v.13]. Attend quia non tantum of refreshment, sed nec de ipso igne optabi tacuit: Introibo in domum tuam in holocaustis. What is holocaustum? Totum incensum, thirst igne divine. Announces holocausts; the body of Christ speaks; The unity of Christ speaks: I will enter your house with burnt offerings. Your fire consumes me completely. Everything that comes from mortal life will be consumed in order to be perfected in eternal life. Then these will be the burnt offerings. 19 [v.14]. And what will happen in the holocausts? I will fulfill my vows to you that distinguished my lips. What distinction is there in these votes? This: that you accuse yourself and praise Him. That you understand that you are a creature and He is Creator. May you see that you are darkness and the illuminator to whom you say: You, O Lord, will illuminate my lamp. My God, you will illuminate my darkness. Because if you had said: Oh soul!, for you and for me my torch shines, you would not distinguish. If you do not distinguish, you do not fulfill the different vows. Fulfill the different vows; recognize yourself as changeable and Him as changeless; confess that without Him you are nothing and that He is perfect without you; that you need Him and He doesn't need you. He neither increases, nor becomes richer, nor is he better equipped. Everything that He performs on your behalf is a better good for you than for Him who does it. And my mouth spoke in my tribulation. How sweet tribulation often is! How necessary! What did his mouth speak there in his tribulation? I will offer you great holocausts. What does pingües or medullos mean? Inside I will have charity; It will not be on the surface; In the most intimate part of the heart will be what I love. There is nothing more interior than our core. The bone is found in us in a more interior place than the flesh, and the marrow is found in a more interior place than the bones. Everyone who superficially worships God tries rather to please men, because, feeling something else inside, he does not offer a rich or mellow holocaust. He who attends to the core of the sacrifice, offers the complete sacrifice, that is, he offers a burnt offering. I will offer you sweet burnt offerings with incense and rams. The rams are the leaders or heads of the Church. The entire body of Christ speaks. This is what he offers to God. What does incense symbolize? The prayer. With incense and rams? In a particular way the rams pray for the flock. I will offer you oxen with goats. We see the oxen threshing and they are offered to God. It is lucky that you say: Come, hear how great things God did for my soul, because all the things that He tells are carried out by His grace in our soul. Listen to the rest of the things he says. 22 [v.18]. If I perceive iniquity in my heart, the Lord does not hear me. Consider now, brothers, how easily, how ordinarily, modest men blame the iniquities of men. He acted evil, he acted infamously, he is an evil man. Maybe he says this by seeing men. See if you do not see iniquity in your heart, lest perhaps what you reproach in others, you think to do, and therefore you impute to him not what he did, but what you found in your heart. Reconsider; be judge for yourself in your heart. See to it that in the secret of your chamber, in the most intimate depths of your heart, where you are alone and He who also sees, you dislike iniquity there so that you may please God. Do not look at her with benign eyes, that is, do not love her, but rather look at her with disdain, despise her and turn away from her. Everything that promises enjoyment to drag you into sin, everything that threatens with sadness to push you to do evil, all of this is nothing, all of it passes away; It is worthy of being despised, of being trampled on, of not being taken into account to accept it. [Sometimes evil is suggested by thoughts or by the words of perverse charlatans, for bad conversations corrupt good morals. You despise them. It is not enough not to keep your eyes on the face, to restrain your tongue; do not look at the heart, that is, do not love, do not consent. It is very common to say look (respicio) for love (diligere). Especially because we say to God respexit me (he looked at me; that is, he loved me). What does nia enim quae enarrat, ipsius gratia fiunt in anima nostra mean? Videte alia quae dicat. 22 [v.18]. Iniquitatem si conspexi in corde meo, non exaudiat Dominus. Consider yourself moda, fratres, quam facile, quam quotidie nomines erubescentes in hominibus iniquitates accusant: Male fecit, perdite fecit, sceleratus homo est: hoc forte propter nomines dicit. Vide si non in corde tuo conspicis iniquitatem; ne forte quod reprehendis in altero, cogites faceré, et ideo in illum clames, non quia fecit, sed quia inventus est. Redi ad te; intus this tibí iudex. Ecce in cubicle tuo abscondito, in ipsa vena intima cordis, ubi tu solus es, et ille qui videt, illic tibi displiceat iniquitas, ut placeas Deo.

He retains the meaning from where he said: Come, hear, and I will speak to all you who fear God how great things he has done for my soul, since he has said the things that you heard, and at last he concludes: Blessed is my God, who has not taken away my prayer and his mercy from me. Thus comes this one who speaks to the resurrection, in which we already find ourselves in hope. What do I say? The one we are already in, because this is our voice. While we are here, let us ask God not to turn away from us our prayer and his mercy, that is, that we pray with perseverance and that he continually pities us. Many languish in prayer. At the beginning of their conversion they pray fervently, but later they do it languidly, coldly, negligently; They do it as if they were safe. The enemy watches, you sleep. The Lord himself says in the Gospel that it is advisable to always pray and never give up. And he offers us the likeness of that wicked judge who feared neither God nor men, who pestered a widow every day begging to be heard; and, impelled by annoyance, he who did not bow down for mercy, gives way; and he says to himself: "If I ignore God or respect men, at least because of the annoyance that this widow causes me every day, I will hear her cause and give her justice. If the wicked judge - says the Lord - did this, will your Father, who is in heaven, not do justice to his chosen ones who claim day and night? I tell you that he will judge quickly." Therefore let us not falter in prayer. What he has to grant, God does not deny, even if he differs. SERMON OF THE PEOPLE

1 [v. 2]. Your charity will remember that the two psalms, 102 and 103, already explained, exhorted our soul to bless the Lord and that with pious song they said: Praise, my soul, the Lord. If in them our soul was exhorted to bless the Lord, it is rightly said in this one that God may have mercy on us and bless us. May our soul bless the Lord and may God bless us. When God blesses us, we grow, and when we bless the Lord, we also grow; Both things benefit us. He does not increase with our blessing nor decrease with our curse. Whoever curses the Lord decreases and whoever blesses him grows. We first obtain the Lord's blessing, and therefore it is natural that we bless him. His blessing is the rain; ours, the fruit. Then through this blessing of ours it is returned as the fruit to the Farmer, God, who rains and gathers. Let us count these things with devotion securi de pollicitatione ipsius non deficiamus orando; et hoc ex benefit ipsius est. Propterea said: Benedictus Deus meus, qui non amovit deprecationem meam, et misericordiam suam a me. Cum videris non a te amotam deprecationem tuam, securus esto, quia non est a te amota mercy eius.

In the things of this visible world, the vine is not a building, and the building is not a vine. But we are the Lord's vineyard because he cultivates us so that we become fruit and we are God's building because he who cultivates us dwells in us. What does the Apostle himself say? I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither he who plants nor he who waters is something, but God, who gives growth. God gives growth. But are these farmers? The one who plants and waters is called a farmer, and the Apostole said: I planted, Apollo watered. Let's ask: How did he do this? And the Apostle himself will answer: Not I, but the grace of God with me. Then wherever you look, whether at the angels, now at the prophets, now at the apostles, God is your farmer. So what are we? Maybe we are workers of that Farmer; and this same thing, receiving the strength from Him and by grace received from Him. Then He Himself cultivates and gives growth. The farmer cultivates the vineyard until he plows it, cleans it, performs the other tasks that belong to the care of the farmer, but he cannot make it rain for his vineyard. And if perhaps he can water it, from whom does he receive this power? He certainly drives the water into the canal, but God fills the fountains. In short, man cannot give growth to the branches of his vineyard, nor form the fruit, nor change the seed, nor temper the season of sterili, non inani voce, sed vero corde. Apertissime enim Deus Pater dictus est agricultural. Apostolus dicit: Dei agriculture estis, Dei aedtficatio estis. In rebus huius mundi visibilibus, vitis non est aedificium, et aedificium non est vinea: nos autem vinea Domini sumus, quia colit nos ad fructum; aedificium Dei sumus, quia qui colit nos habitat in nobis. Et quid ait Idem Apostolus? Ego plantan, Apollo rigavit; sed Deus incrementum dedit. Ergo ñeque qui plantat est aliquid, ñeque qui rigat; sed qui incrementum dat Deus (1 Cor 3:6-9). Ule ergo incrementum dat. Numquid forte isti sunt agricolae? Agricola enim dicitur qui plantat, qui rigat: dixit autem Apostolus, Ego plantavi, Apollo rigavit. Quaerimus unde ipse hoc fecerit?

In various ways men want to be blessed by God. Some want to be blessed to have a house full of the things of this life; others, to retain the health of the body, being free from diseases; others, if they are sick, to regain health; Others, desiring to have children, and perhaps saddened by not having them, long to be blessed to obtain posterity. Who can enumerate the different desires of men who desire to be blessed by the Lord God? But who among us is to say that he has not been blessed by God or when agriculture provides him with fruits, or when someone's house abounds with temporal goods, or when it helps the health of the body or so that he does not lose what he has or to recover what he has lost? The fertility of women, the chaste desire of those who desire children, to whom does it belong but to the Lord God? The one who created when he is; securi sumus. Forte ait aliquis, Tu dicis agricolam nostrum esse Deum: imo ego Apostólos agricultural dico, qui dixerunt, Ego plantavi, Apollo rigavit. Si ego dico, nemo credat: si Christus dicit, vae qui non credit. Quid ergo Dominus Christus ait? Ego sum vitis, vos sarmenta, Pater meus agricola (lo 15,5.1). Et quis enumerate diverse vote hominum se a Domino Deo benedici cupientium? Quis autem nostrum dicturus est non esse illam Dei benedictionem, si vel agriculture ei fructum ferat, vel domus cuiusque abundet copy rerum temporalium, vel ipsa corporis salus, aut teneatur ne amittatur, aut amissa reparetur? It is not enough to tell us that these things are executed by God, granted by God. Only He executes them, only He grants them. What would happen if God did these things and someone other than God did them? He does them and He alone. Without reason these things are asked of men or demons; Whatever good things the enemies of God receive, they receive from Him; and, even when they are asked of others, when they receive them, they receive them, without knowing it, from Him. Just as, when men are punished and think that they are punished by others, being it by Him, being ignorant of it, so also, when they are recreated, filled with benefits, saved, delivered, and, being ignorant of it, they attribute it to men, demons or angels, yet they have only obtained it from Him, in whom the power is found. of all things. We have said this, brothers, so that everyone who also desires these earthly things, whether to remedy a need or to cure an illness, desires them only from Him who is the source of all good and the Creator and restorer of all things. 3. But there are some gifts that God also gives to his enemies and others that He reserves only for His friends. What are the gifts that I enumerated? supplied with the things necessary for life, not only the good are freed from danger or cured of illnesses; nor do only the good have children, or money, or other things convenient for this temporary and passing life.

the bad ones well and sometimes the good ones lack them. The bad ones also lack them, and sometimes more of them than the good ones; others, more to the good than the bad. God wanted these temporal things to be possessed indiscriminately by both, because if He had only granted them to the good, the bad would judge that God should be worshiped by them; On the contrary, if he had given them only to the bad, the good, but weak ones, would be wary of converting, lest they perhaps lack them. For the weak soul still falters in the kingdom of God; That is why the Lord, our farmer, must nourish it. The tree that already resists storms with its strength, when it sprang from the earth it was grass. Not only does the Farmer know how to clean and prune strong trees, but also protect the tender ones at their birth with hedges. Therefore, dear ones, as I began to tell you, if these things were given only to the good, everyone would want to convert to God by receiving them; and, if he only gave them to the bad, the weak would fear converting so as not to lose what they would only have by being bad. Then they have been given indifferently to the good and the bad. On the other hand, if only the good were deprived of them, the weak would be wary of converting to God; If only the bad ones, one would think that this was the only penalty with which they are punished. When he gives them to the good, he comforts the wayfarers. When he gives them to the bad, he warns the good to desire other, better goods that they will not have in common with the bad. In short, he takes them away from the good when he wants so that they can ask themselves how strong they are and see if those who perhaps did not know themselves can now say: The Lord gave it to me, the Lord gave it to me.

Ad hoc dixerimus haec, fratres, ut quisquís etiam ista terrena forte, vel propter supplementa necessitatis, vel propter aliquam infirmitatem desiderat, nonnisi ab illo desideret, qui est fons omnium bonorum, et creator et recreator Universorum. 3. Sed alia sunt dona quae dat Deus et inimicis suis, alia quae non servat nisi amicis suis. Quae sunt dona quae dat inimicis suis? Ea quae numeravi. Non enim soli boni plenas habent domos rebus necessariis; aut soli boni, vel salvi sunt, vel ab aegritudine convalescunt; aut soli boni filios habent, soli boni pecuniam, soli boni caetera apta huic vitae temporali atque transeunti. Habent haec et malí, et alíquando

desunt bonis: sed desunt et malis, et pletumque istis magis quam illis; aliquando illis quam istis potius abundant. Permixta ista temporalia Deus esse voluit; quia si bonis solis ea daret, putarent et mali propter haec colendum Deum; rursus si ea solis malis daret, timerent boni infirmi convertedí, ne ista illis forte deessent. Est enim adhuc anima infirma minus capax regni Dei; I will nourish illam debent Deus agricultural noster. Nana et quae arbor iam tempestates robore sustinet, cum de terra nasceretur, herba erat. Novit ergo ille agricultural non solum robustas arbores putare atque purgare; sed etiam teñeras in recenti ortu sepire. Propterea, dilectissimi, ut dicere coeperam, si solis bonis darentur ista, omnes propter haec accipienda vellent convertí ad Deum: rursus si solis malis darentur, timerent infirmi, ne cum converterentur, amitterent quod soli mali haberent. Permixte data sunt et bonis et malis. Rursus si solis bonis auferrentur, idem ille timor esset infirmorum, ne converterentur ad Deum: rursus si solis malis auferrentur, ipsa sola poena putaretur qua mali plectuntur. Quod ergo dat ea bonis, consolatur itinerant: quod dat ea et malis, admonet bonds ut alia desiderent, quae non habent cum malis communia. Rursus bonis aufert ea quando vult, ut interrogent se de suis viribus; et inveniant se, qui forte latebant se, utrum iam possint dicere: Dominus dedit, Dominas abstulit; sicut Domino placuit,

The Lord gave it to me, the Lord took it from me; He took from me what he gave, but he did not remove the giver from me. The blessed and by no means simple soul does not cling to earthly things nor does it lie on the ground with its wings folded due to the garter, but, freed by the magnificence of the virtues, it rejoices in the spacious auras of heaven supported by the two wings of double love; and likewise she sees that what weighed her has been taken away, not what held her in the air, and, for the same reason, she says confidently: The Lord gave it to me, the Lord took it from me; As it pleased God, so it was done; blessed be the name of the Lord. He gave and took away; He who gave and took away what he gave remains; May his name be blessed. For this, then, the good ones are removed. But so that perhaps some weakling may not say: When will I be able to have as much virtue as holy Job had? You admire the strength of the tree because you were recently born. The one you see now so large, under whose branches and shadow you cool off, was a wand. Do you fear that these things will be taken away from you when you become such? See that they will be taken away from the bad ones. Why do you delay the conversion? What you fear to lose by being good, perhaps you will have to lose by being bad. If you lose it by being good, you have the Comforter, who took it from you. The ark is empty of gold, but the heart is full of faith. Outwardly you are poor, but inwardly you are rich. With you you carry the riches, which you will not lose even if you emerge naked from the shipwreck. If perhaps, being bad, you have to lose it, why don't you find this loss good, since many times you also see the damage suffered?

to the bad ones? These are hurt with greater damage, because their house is empty, and their conscience is even more empty. Any evil person who has lost these things will not have externally what he had nor will he have a place to rest internally. He flees from where he suffered harm, from where he boasted with the ostentation of his wealth before the public eye; He can no longer boast in the sight of men nor does he return to his interior, because he has nothing. He did not imitate the ant; He did not gather grain for himself in the summer. What did I say when I mentioned summer? That it was his summer when he was in the prosperity of life, when the prosperity of the century surrounded him, when he was idle, when he was called happy by men. If he had heard the word of God, he would have imitated the ant, because he would have collected food and hidden it inside. The test of tribulation will come, the winter of marasmus, the storm of fear, the cold of sadness, or some harm or danger to health, or some deprivation of those close to us, or some dishonor and humiliation, will come upon us, and then it will be winter; but the ant turns its eyes to what it collected in the summer, and there in its hiding place, where no one sees it, it delights in the summer's work. When she collected the grains during the summer, everyone saw her; When she feeds on them in the winter, no one sees her. What does this mean? Observe the ant of God; He appears every day, goes to the temple of the Lord, prays, listens to the reading, sings the hymns, meditates on what he heard, reflects within himself and hides in his heart the grains that he gathered on the threshing floor. These things that are now said are put into practice by those who hear learnedly. Everyone sees them go to church,

What are the vides et malo pati damnum? Sed maiore illi damno feriuntur: inanis est domus, inanior conscientia est. Quisquís malus ista perdiderit, non habet foris quod teneat, non habet intus ubi requiescat. Fugit hic ubi damnum passus est, ubi se ad oculos hominum de divitiarum ostentatione iactabat; iam se in oculis hominum iactare non potest: ad se intro non redit, quia nihil habet. Non est imitatus formicam; non sibi collegit grana, cum aestas esset (Prov 6,6, et 30,25). Quid dixi, cum aestas esset? Cum esset vitae tranqui Hitas, cum esset saeculi huius erga illum prosperitas, quando ei vacabat, quando felix vocabatur ab ómnibus, aestas ipsius erat. Imitaretur formicam, si audiret verbum Dei; colligeret grana, et intus reconderet. Venerat tentatio tribulationis, supervenerat hiems torporis, tempestas timoris, frigus tristitiae, sive damnum esset, sive aliquod salutis periculum, sive aliqua orbits suorum, sive aliqua exhonoratio et humiliatio; hiems erat: redit formica ad id quod aestate collegit; et intus in secreto suo, ubi nemo videt, aestivis laboribus recreatur. Quando sibi ista colligebat aestate, videbant omnes: cum his pascitur hieme, nullus videt. Quid est hoc? Vide formicam Dei: surgit quotidie, currit ad ecclesiam Dei, orat, audit lectionem, hymnum cantat, ruminat quod audivit, apud se cogitat, recondit intus grana collecta de area. Haec ipsa quae moda dicuntur qui prudenter.

May God arise and let your enemies be dispersed. It has already happened, "because Christ has risen, who is God over all things, worthy to be blessed forever," and his enemies, the Jews, were scattered among all the nations. Now they hate, but they fear; and, overcome by the same fear, they do what follows: And let those who hated him flee from his presence. The flight of the soul is fear. Where will I go from your spirit and where will I flee from your face? Then they flee with their spirit, not with their body; namely, fearing, not hiding. Hence he said to his pursuers: In a little while you will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds. After having said: God is in his holy place, as if we had asked him in what place, since He is in everyone and does not contain any bodily space, he then adds: So that we do not look for Him outside of ourselves, but rather so that we deserve that He deigns to dwell in us, that we live in the house of a single customs. This is the holy place of God that men often seek in order to have a place in which hominum turbant, Turbabuntur a facie eius, patris orpbanorum et iudicis viduarum. Desolatos enim putant, a quibus plerumque gladio verbi Dei, et parentes a filiis, et mariti ab uxoribus separantur (Mt 10,34.35): sed habent consolationem destituti atque viduati patris orpbanorum et iudicis viduarum; habent eius consolationem qui ei dicunt, Quoniam pater meus et mater mea dereliquerunt me; Dominus autem assumpsit me (Ps 26,10): et qui speraverunt in Domino, persistent in orationibus nocte ac die (1 Tim 5,5); a cuius facie illi turbabuntur, cum viderint se nihil proficere, quoniam totus mundus post eum abiit (lo 12,19). 7 [v.7]. Nam de his orphanis et viduis, id est spei saecularis societate destitutis, Dominus sibi templum fabricat: de quo consequenter dicit, Dominus, in loco sancto suo.

Quis enim sit locus eius aperuit, cum ait, Deus qui inbabitare facit unius modi in domo: unanimous, unum sentientes: iste est locus sanctus Domini. Cum enim dixisset, Dominus in loco sancto suo: tanquam requireremus in quo loco, cum ille ubique sit totus, et nullus eum contineat corporalium spatiorum locus, illico subiecit; ne quaeramus eum absque nobis; sed potius unius modi inhabitants in domo, mereamur ut habitare etiam ipse dignetur in nobis. This is locus sanctus Domini, quem plerique nomines quaerunt, ut habeant ubi orantes exaudiantur. Sint ipsi ergo quod quaerunt; et quae dicunt in cordibus suís, id est in talibus cubilibus suis, compungantur (Ps 4,5),

praying they be heard. Be themselves the place you seek; and what they say in their hearts, that is, in their beds, compels them, living in the house of the same customs so that they may be inhabited by the Lord of the great house and be heard within themselves. For this is the great house, in which there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay, and among these, some are, certainly, for honor and others for contumelia. If some have cleansed themselves (ceased to be vessels of ignominy), they will dwell in the house of one custom and will be the holy place of the Lord. Because just as in a great palace its lord does not dwell in any part of it, but in the most honorable and hidden place, so God does not dwell in all those who are in his house, since he does not dwell in the vessels of ignominy. His holy place is those men whom he makes live in the house with a single way of being or a single custom. Those called tropoi (way of being) in Greek are translated in Latin as modi or mores (modes or customs). Nor is it written in the Greek codex what is written in Latin: qui inbabitare facit (he who causes to dwell), but only habitare facit (makes to dwell). Then the Lord dwells in his holy place. What is this place? The Lord is done to him. For God makes those with the same way of being live in the house. This is his holy place. 8. Nam sicut in magna hominis domo, non in qualicumque loco eius requiescit dominus eius, sed in aliquo utique secretiore et honoratiore loco: sic Deus non in ómnibus qui in domo eius sunt habitat (non enim habitat in vasis contumeliae); sed locus sanctus eius sunt quos habitare jacit unius modi, vel unius moris in domo.

Then, when you were passing through the desert, when you were preached to the nations, the earth was moved, that is, earthly men were moved to faith. But how was he moved? Perhaps someone here remembers the time when God led his people through the desert, leading the children of Israel; by day, in a column of cloud, and by night, in a column of fiery brilliance; and think that distilling the heavens in the sight of God is raining manna on the people, and also believe that the following was said: Mount Sinai in the sight of the God of Israel, who secretes spontaneous rain, O God, for your inheritance, because Goddess Moses spoke on Mount Sinai when she gave him the law. So that the manna is the spontaneous rain that God secreted or prepared for his inheritance, that is, for his people, since he only fed him in this way and not the other nations; so that what is said sed eis qui noverunt opera eius intueri. Non enim ea nunc opera dico, quae conspicua sunt omnibus, caelum, et terram, et mare, et universe quae in eis sunt; sed opera quibus educit compeditos in fortitudine, similiter amaneantes qui habitant in sepulcris, et facit eos unius morís inhabite in domo. Sic egreditur coram populo suo, id est coram eis qui istam gratiam eius intelligunt. Denique sequitur: Cum transires in deserto, terra mota est.

Desertum erant Gentes, quae ignorabant Deum: desertum etat, ubi lex nulla ab ipso Deo data erar, ubi nulli Prophetae habítaverant, Dominumque esse venturum praedixerant. Cum ergo transires in deserto, cum praedicareris in Gentibus, terra mota est, terreni nomines ad fidem excitati sunt. Sed unde mota est? Etenim caeli distillaverunt a facie Dei. Forsitan hic aliquis recolat illud tempus, quando in deserto Deus transibat coram populo suo, coram filiis Israel, die in column nubis, night in fulgore ignis (Ex 13,21); et hoc esse sentiat quod caeli distillaverunt a facie Dei, quoniam manna pluit populo suo (Ib. 16,13); hoc etiam esse quod sequitur, Mons Sina a facie Dei Israel, pluviam voluntaryam segregans, Deus, haereditati tuae, quia in monte Sina locutus est Deus ad Moysen, quando Legem dedit (Ib. 19,18, etc.): ut manna sit pluvia voluntary quam segregavit Deus haereditati suae, id est populo suo: quia solos eos ita pavit, non et caetetas Gentes: ut quod deinde dicit, Et infírmala est, ipsa baereditas

By infirmata intelligatur; quoniam murmurantes, manna fastidiosi respuerunt, desiderantes escás carnium, et ea quibus vesci in Aegipto consueverant (Num 11,5.6). Sed in his verbis si proprietas tantummodo litterae, non spiritualis requírendus est intellectus, oportet ut ostendatur secundum proprietatem corporalem, qui tune compediti, quique etiam inhabitants in sepulcris educti sunt in fortitudine. Deinde si ille populus, illa scilicet haereditas Dei, annoyance manna respuens infirmata est, non debuit sequi, Tu vero perfecisti eam; sed, Tu vero percussisti eam. Deo quippe offenso per illa murmura atque fastidia, ingens plague secuta est (Ib. 33). Omnia quippe illa in figura contingebant in illis (1 Cor 10:11); doñee aspiraret dies, et removerentur umbrae (Song 2:17). 10. Aperiat itaque nobis pulsantibus Dominus; et mysteriorum eius, quantum ipse digntur, secret pandantur. Etenim ut terra mota esset ad fidem, cum in desettum Gentium transiret Evangelium, caeli iistillaverunt a facie Dei. Hi sunt caeli, de quibus in alio psalmo canitur: Caeli enarrant gloriam Dei. De his quippe paulo post ibi dicitur: Non sunt loquelae ñeque sermones, quorum non audiantnr voices eorum: in

His voice resonates throughout the earth and his words resonate throughout all the ends of the globe. However, so much glory should not be attributed to these heavens as if that grace had come through men to the desert of the nations so that the earth might be moved to faith. For the heavens did not distill by themselves, but by the grace of God, who, without a doubt, dwelt in them "and made them dwell in the house of the same customs." They are also the mountains of which it is said: I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me. And so that it would not appear that the psalmist had trusted in men, he then added: My help comes from God, who made heaven and earth. It is also said to Him in another place: You who illuminate wonderfully from the eternal mountains; although from the eternal mountains, nevertheless, you are the one who illuminates. For the same reason, it is also said here that the heavens distilled, but by the grace of God. For they were saved through faith, and this was not their own work, but a gift from God, since they are not saved by works, so that no one can become arrogant. We are, therefore, the workmanship of Him who makes dwelling in the house of one custom. 11. But what's next? Mount Sinai in view of the God of Israel. Should it be understood as "distilled," so that what he called heaven he would also have wanted to designate as Mount Sinai, just as we already said that he called the heavens mountains? Even taking it in this sense, we should not be concerned about having said mountain and not mountains, since it was said there heaven, and not heaven; for when writing in another psalm: The heavens sing the glory of omnem terram exiit sonus eorum, et in fines orbis terrae verba eorum (Ps 18:2-3). Nec tamen istis caelis tanta gloria ttibuenda est, tanquam ab hominibus illa gratia venerit in desertum Gentium, ut terra moveretur ad fidem. Non enim caeli a seipsis distillaverunt; sed a facie Dei, utique inhabitantis eos, et facientis eos inhabitare unius moris in domo. Ipsi sunt enim et montes, de quibus dicitur: Levavi oculos meos ad montes, ande veniet auxilium mihi. Et tamen ne in hominibus spem posuisse videretur, continuo subiecit: Auxilium meum a Domino, qui fecit caelum et terram (Ps 120,1.2). Ei quippe alio loco dicitur, llluminans tu admirabiliter, a montibus aeternis (Ps 75,5): quamvis a montibus aeternis, tamen illuminans tu. Sic et hic, caeli distillaverunt; thirst, a facie Dei.

Et ipsi enim salvi facti sunt pet fidem, et hoc non ex seipsis; sed Dei donum est: non ex operibus, ne forte quis extollatur. An subaudiendum est, distillavit: ut quod vocavit caelorum nomine, hoc voluerit intelligi nomine etiam montis Sina; sicut diximus eos vocari montes, qui vocati sunt caeli? What follows in the psalm: but you perfected it, refers to the law, because, according to what we said, it was perfected, that is, it was fulfilled. The Lord testifies to this, saying in the Gospel: I did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it. Hence it is that the Apostle, who had said that the law was weakened by the flesh, because the flesh does not work what is done by the spirit, that is, by spiritual grace, also says: That the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit; that is, because you perfected it, because the fullness of the law is charity, and the charity of God is spread in our hearts not by ourselves, but by the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. Therefore this is you perfected it, if the perfection of the law is understood. If the perfection of the inheritance is understood, the meaning is easier. If it was said that the inheritance of God was weakened, that is, the people of God when the law was given to them, because the law was given so that sin would abound, then also what follows in the psalm: you perfected it, is understood by what, likewise, follows in the Apostle: where crime abounded, grace abounded all the more. Because, as the crime abounded, their weaknesses multiplied and then accelerated, since they groaned and prayed that, with God helping them, they would fulfill what he told them they could not fulfill. 12. These words contain another meaning that seems more probable to me. He knew what was said: I will rather boast of my weaknesses. He knew what was said: Do not be proud, but fear. He knew what was said: Give grace to the humble. And she became weak, but you perfected her, because virtue is perfected in weakness. In truth, some codices, both Latin and Greek, do not write Mount Sinai, but in the sight of the God of Sinai, in the sight of the God of Israel; that is, the heavens dropped before God; and as if asked: Of what God?, he says: In the sight of the God of Sinai, in the sight of the God of Israel. That is, before the God who gave the law to the people of Israel. Why did the heavens drop before God, before this God, if it were not because what was predicted was fulfilled: He who gave the law will give the blessing? The law, with which I terrify him who presumes on human strength, and the blessing, with which he frees him who hopes in God. "You, O God, perfected your inheritance," because it was weakened in itself in order to be perfected by you. 13 [v. l l ]. Your animals will live there. Yours, not his; those subjected to you, do not free them in themselves; those who need you, not those who believe themselves to be enough. Sweetness, of which it was said elsewhere: The Lord will give sweetness and our earth will give its fruit, consists in doing good out of love, not out of fear; not for fear of punishment, but for the delight of justice. This is true and sensible freedom. But God prepared this for the poor, not for the opulent, for whom this poverty is shameful. Of these it was said in another place: It is ridicule for the rich and contempt for the proud. He called those he called rich arrogant. 14 {v.12}. The Lord will give word, that is, he will give food to his animals that live in his house. But what will these animals who are given the word do? What else but what follows: they will evangelize with great power? With what power if not with the strength with which he freed them when they were chained? Perhaps I also point out here the virtue with which the evangelizers performed great wonders. 15 [v. 13]. Who will give the evangelizers a word with great power? The king, he says, of the armies of the Beloved. Therefore the Father is the king of the armies of the Son. When the Beloved is written it does not indicate who the Beloved is, it is understood par excellence the only Son. Perhaps the Son himself is king of his armies, that is, of the armies that serve him? For the king of hosts will give a word with great power to the evangelizers, and of whom it is said: The Lord of hosts is the king of glory. Not having said king of his armies, but king of the armies of the Beloved, is a very common phrase in the holy Scriptures,

as anyone can see. This appears mainly where the proper name is recorded so that there can be no doubt at all that it is the same one being spoken of. Such a mode of speech is found in many places in the Pentateuch; for example: And Moses did this and that, as the Lord commanded Moses, etc., etc. He did not say, according to our way of speaking: And Moses did as the Lord commanded him, but: And Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses. As if one were the Moses who was commanded and another who acted, although it is the same. These locutions are hardly found in the New Testament. However, here we have it in what the Apostle says: About his Son who was born to him of the lineage of David according to the flesh, who was predestined Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification by virtue of the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord. (Here it appears) as if one were the Son of God, who was born of the lineage of David according to the flesh, and another Jesus Christ, our Lord; being so that it is one and the same. This way of speaking is frequent in the books of the Old Testament. Therefore, when some passages appear somewhat obscure, they must be understood as clearer ones that deal with the same subject. The locution of this passage of the psalm that I now present is somewhat obscure. For if it were said: Jesus Christ, king of the armies of Jesus Christ, it would be as clear as that: Moses did as the Lord commanded Moses; But since it was said that he was king of the armies of the Beloved, it is not easy for him to be king of the armies who is also the Beloved. then king

illius empower yourself. Egens est enim, quoniam infirmatus est, ut perficiatur: agnovit se indigentem, ut repleatur. Ipsa est enim vera et sana libertas. Be Dominus hoc genti paravit, non abundanti, cui opprobrio est ista paupertas; de qualibus alibi dicitur: Opprobrium bis qui abundant, et despectio superbis (Ps 122.4). Sed quid operabuntur haec animalia, quibus dabit verbum? quid nisi quod sequitur? Evangeliía-ntihus virtutefine. Qua virtute, nisi fortitudine illa in qua educit compeditos? Fortasse etiam virtutem hic dicat illam, qua evangelizers mirabilia signa fecerunt. 15 [v.13]. Quis ergo dabit verbum evangelizantibus virtute Fine? Rex, inquit, virtutum Dilecti. Pater ergo est rex virtutum Filii, Dilectus enim, quando non ponitur quis dilectus, per antonomasiam Filius unicus intelligitur. An virtutum suarum rex ipse Elius; virtutum scilicet sibi servientium? quia virtute fines evangelizantibas dabit verbum rex virtutum, de quo dictum est, Dominas virtutum, ipse est rex gloriae (Ps 23:10). Quod autem non dixit, Rex virtutum suarum, sed,

Rex virtutum Dilecti, locutio est in Scripturis usitatissima, si quis advertat: quod ibi máxime apparet, ubi etíam proprium nomen exprimitur, ut eumdem esse de quo dicitur, dubitari omnino non possit. Qualis et illa in Pentateucho multis locis invenitur: Et fecit Moyses illud atque illud, sicut praecepit Dominus Moysi (Num 17,11, etc., sec. LXX). Non dixit quod usitatum est in locutionibus nostris, Et fecit Moyses sicut praecepit ei Dominus; thirst, Fecit Moyses sicut praecepit Dominus Moysi; quasi alius sit Moyses cui praecepit, et alius Moyses qui fecit, cum idem ipse sit. Such locutions in New Testament difficult reperiuntur. Inde est tamen quod Apostolus ait: De Filio suo, qui factus est ei ex semine David secundum carnem, qui praedestinatus est Filius Dei in virtute secundum Spiritum sanctificationis ex resurrectione mortuorum lesu Cbristi Domini nostri (Rom 1,3.4): tanauam alius sit Filius Dei qui factus est ex semine David secundum carnem, et alius Iesus Christus Dominus noster, cum sit unus atque Idem. In veteribus autem libris crebra est ista locutio: et ideo quando subobscure fit, ex manifestis sui generis exemplis intelligenda est; sicut hoc loco psalmi huius quem tractamus, subobscure facta est. Nam si diceretur Iesus Christus, rex virtutum lesu Christi, tam aperta esset quam illa, Fecit Moyses sicut praecepit Dominus Moysi: quia vero dictum est, Rex virtutum Dilecti, non facile est ut occurrat ipsum esse regem virtutum, qui est et Dilectus. Rex ergo

of the armies of the Beloved can be understood as if he had said king of his armies, because Christ is also king of the armies, and, likewise, the Beloved is Jesus Christ himself. However, this sense does not bind so much that it cannot be taken in another, because it can also be understood that the Father is king of the armies of his beloved Son, to whom the Beloved himself says: All my things are yours, and yours are mine. If anyone asks: Can God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, be called king? I do not know that anyone dares to strip him of this name, when the Apostle says: Honor and glory to the king of the ages, immortal and invisible, only God. Because even if this were said of the Trinity itself, God the Father is in it. If we do not carnally understand the words, O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king's Son, I do not know what else they applied to if not to his Son. Therefore the Father is also king. Hence the verse of this king psalm of the armies of the Beloved can be understood in both ways. Therefore, after having said: The Lord will give the word with great power to the evangelizers, as by the same power he is governed by Him and is subject to Him for whom it is given, He Himself says: The Lord, who gives the word with great power to the evangelizers, is king of the armies of the Beloved. 16. Then it continues: Of the Beloved, who divides the spoils for the beauty of the house. The repetition of the word of the Beloved is done to ponder. However, this repetition is not found in all codices. The most careful ones write it down, placing a little star called an asterisk. By these signs virtutum Dilecti, sic intelligi potest, ac si diceretur, rex virtutum suarum, quia et rex virtutum est Christus, et Dilectus est idem ipse Christus. Quamvis non habeat iste sensus tantam necessitatem, ut aliud non valeat accipi: quia et Pater potest intelligi rex virtutum Filii sui dilecti, cui dicit ipse Dilectus, Omnia mea tua sunt, et tua mea (lo 17,10). Quod si forte quaeritur utrum Deus Domini Iesu Christi Pater etiam rex dici possit, nescio utrum quisquam audeat hoc ab eo nomen auferre, ubi Apostolus dicit: Regi autem saeculorum immortali, invisihili, soli Deo (1 Tim 1,17).

Quia etsi hoc de ipsa Trinitate dictum est, ibi est et Deus Pater. Si autem non carnaliter intelligimus, Deus, iuiicium tuum regi da, et iustitiam tuam filio regis (Ps 71,2); nescio utrum aliud aliquid dictum est quam, Filio tuo. Rex ergo est et Pater. Unde versiculus iste psalmi huius, Rex virtutum Dilecti, utroque modo intelligi potest. Cum itaque dixisset, Dominus dabit verbum evangelizantibus virtute malta; quia ipsa virtus ab eo regitur, eique militat a quo datur, ipse, inquit, Dominus qui dabit verbum evangelizantibus virtute tumba, rex est virtutum Dilecti. 16. Deinde sequitur: Dilecti, et speciei domus dividere spolia. Repeated pertinet ad commendationem: quanquam istam repetitionem non omnes codices habeant, et eam diligentiores stella apposita praenotant, quae signa vocantur asterisci; quibus agnosci volunt ea non esse in interpretatione Septuagint, sed esse in hebraeo, quae talibus insigniuntur

It is intended to make known that where they are found, a word is missing in the text of the Septuagint, but not in the Hebrew text. Whether the word dilecti, of the Beloved, is repeated or taken as having been said once, I think that what follows must be understood: that he divides the spoils for the beauty of the house, as if saying that he divides the spoils of the Beloved for the beauty of the house, that is, that the spoils of the Beloved are to be divided. Since Christ beautified the house, that is, the Church, dividing the spoils for it (and thus made it beautiful), just as the body is beautiful by the distribution of the members. The belongings that are taken from enemies who have been defeated are called spoils. The Gospel makes this known to us where we read: No one enters the strong man's house to take away his belongings if he does not first tie up the strong man. Then Christ tied the devil with spiritual chains, defeating death and ascending from hell to heaven. He tied him with the sacrament of his incarnation, because, despite finding nothing worthy of death in him, he nevertheless allowed Him to kill him, and, tying him for this, he took his belongings like spoils. The devil worked in the children of disbelief, whom he used at his will through perfidy. The Lord cleansing these articles or vessels with the remission of sins, sanctifying these spoils taken from the enemy, torn down and bound, he divided them for the beauty of his house, constituting some apostles, others prophets, others pastors and doctors in the work of the evangelical ministry for the edification of the body of Christ. For in the same way that the body is one and has many members, and, being many, all the members of the body are notis. Sed sive repetatur, sive semel dictum accipiatur quod positum est, Dilecti; sic intelligendum puto quod sequitur, et speciei domus dividere spolia, ac si diceretur, Dilecti etiam speciei domus dividere spolia, id est, Dilecti etiam ad dividenda spolia. Speciosam quippe domum, id est Ecclesiam Christus fecit, dividendo illi spolia; sicut speciosum est corpus distributione membrorum. Spolia porro dicuntur quae victis hostibus detrahuntur. Hoc quid sit Evangelium nos admonet, ubi legimus: Nemo intrat in iomum jortis, ut vasa eius diripiat, nisi prius alligaverit fortem (Mt 12:29).

Alligavit ergo diabolum Christus spiritualibus vinculis; surpassing mortem, et super cáelos ab inferís ascending: alligavit eum sacramento incarnationis suae, quod nihil in eo reperiens morte dignum, tamen est permissus occidere; ac sic alligato abstulit tanquam spolia vasa eius. Operabatur quippe in filiis diffidentiae (Eph 2,2), quorum infidelítate utebatur ad voluntatem suam. Haec vasa Dominus mundans remissione peccatorum, haec spolia sanctificans hosti erepta prostrato atque alligato, divisit ea speciei domus suae; alios constituens apostólos, alios prophetas, alios pastors et doctors in opus ministerii, in aedificationem corporis Christi (Eph 4,11.12). Sicut enim unum corpus est, et membra plana habet; omnia autem membra corporis cum sint plana, unum est corpus: sic et Christus. Numquid omnes apostoli? numquid omnes prophetae? numquid omnes virtutes? num-

one body, so also Christ. Are they all apostles, all prophets, all virtues, all have the gift of healing, all speak languages, all interpret? However, all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who gives in particular to each one as he wills. This is the beauty of the house for which he divides the spoils so that the lover of it, adorned with this beauty, may exclaim: O Lord, I loved the beauty of your house. 17 [v.14}. Now in what follows he addresses the same members with whom he constituted the beauty of the house, saying: If you slept in the midst of the lots, silver wings of a dove, and on your backs, with yellowness of gold. Here we must first investigate the order of the words to see how the thought ends, which is pending when he says: If you slept. Then it must be investigated whether in what follows: silver wings of a dove, the word pennae is found in plural or singular number; that is, if it is to be translated by wings or by wing. The Greek text completely excludes the singular number, since it recorded it in the plural. But it is not yet clear whether it should be translated by wings, in the nominative, or in this way, in the vocative: Oh you, wings!, so that it seems that we are speaking to the same wings. Or if these words are to be joined to the previous ones, and thus the sentence is concluded, so that the order is this: The Lord will give the evangelizers a word with great power if you sleep in the midst of the lots, oh you silver wings of a dove!; O they join those that follow, so that it is said: If you sleep in the midst of the lots, the silver wings of the dove will be white as the snow in the Selquid omnes dona habent curationum? numquid omnes linguis loquuntur? numquid omnes interpretantur? Omnia autem haec operatur tinus atque idem Spiritus, dividends propria unicuique prout vult (1 Cor 12, 12.29-30.11). Et haec est species domus, cui spolia dividuntur; ut amator eius hac pulchritudine accensus exclaimed: Domine, dilexi decorem domus tuae (Ps 25,8). 17 [v.14]. Iam in eo quod sequitur, se ad ipsa membra, de quibut fit species domus, alloquenda convertit, they say: Si dormiatis inter media cleros, pennae columbae deargentatae, et inter scapulas eius in viriditate auri.

Prius hic quaerendus est ordo verborum quomodo finiatur sententia; quae utique pendet, cum dicitur, Si dormiatis: deinde quod ait, pennae columbae deargentatae, utrum singulari numero intelligendum est, huius pennae; an plurali, hae pennae. Sed singularem numerum graecus excludit, ubi omnino pluraliter hoc positum legitur. Sed adhuc incertum est utrum, hae pennae; an, o vos pennae, ut ad ipsas pennas loqui videatur. Utrum ergo verbis quae praecesserunt finiatur ista sententia, ut ordo sit, Dominus dabit verbum evangelizantihus virtute tumba, si dormiatis inter media cleros, o vos pennae columbae deargentatae: an his quae sequuntur, ut ordo sit, Si dormiatis inter media cleros, pennae columbae deargentatae nive dealbabuntur in Sel-

mon; that is, the same wings will whiten if you sleep among the lots. Thus it would be understood that this was said to those who, like spoils, are divided for the beauty of the house. That is to say, if you sleep in the midst of the lots, O you who are divided for the beauty of the house, through the manifestation of the Spirit, to be useful, so that to some it is given by the Spirit to speak of wisdom; to another, he speaks of science according to the same Spirit; to another, faith; to another, graces of healing in the same Spirit and the other gifts of which the Apostle speaks. Then, if you sleep in the midst of the lots, then the silver wings of the dove will be white as the snow on (Mount) Selmon. It can also be stated like this: If you, silver-winged doves, sleep in the midst of the lots, you will be whitened by snow in Selmon, meaning men, who receive the remission of sins through grace. Hence it is also said of the same Church in the Song of Songs: Who is this that rises whitewashed? This promise was received from God through the prophet, who says: If your sins were the color of a game, I will make them white as snow. It can also be understood in such a way that in what was said silver wings of a dove it is understood that you will be; so that the meaning is this: Oh you who are divided, like spoil, for the beauty of the house!, if you sleep in the midst of the lots, you will be the silver wings of a dove, that is, you will rise to the heights, remaining, nevertheless, united to the constitution or connection of the Church. I believe that no other silver dove can be better understood here than that of which it was said: Only one is my dove. It is silver because it is adocmon: id est, ipsae pennae dealbabuntur, si dormiatis inter media cleros: ut illis hoc dicere intelligatur, qui speciei domus tanquam spolia dividuntur; id est, Si dormiatis intermedias cleros, o vos qui dividimini speciei domus, per manifestationem Spiritus ad utilitatem, ut alii quidem detur per Spiritum sermo sapientiae, alii sermo scientiae secundum eumdem Spiritum, alii fides, alii genera curationum in eodem Spiritu, et caetera (1 Cor 12,7.9): si ergo vos dormiatis inter media cleros, tune pennae columbae deargentatae nive dealbabuntur in Selmón.

Potest et sic: If you, pennae columbae deargentatae. dormiatis inter media cleros, nive dealbabuntur in Selmón, ut subintelligantur homines, qui per gratiam remissionem accipiunt peecatorum. Unde etiam de ipsa Écclesia dicitur in Cántico canticorum: Quae est ista quae ascendit dealbata? (Song 3,6, sec. LXX). Promissio quippe Dei íenetur, per Prophetam dicetis: Si fuerint peccata vestra tanquam phaenicium, sicut level dealbabo? (Is 1,18). Potest et sic intelligi, ut in eo quod dictum est, pennae columbae deargentatae, subaudiatur, eritis; ut iste sit sensus: O vos qui tanquam spolia speciei domus dividimini, si dormiatis inter media cleros, pennae columbae deargentatae eritis; id est, in altiora elevabimini, compagini tamen Ecclesiae cohaerentes. Nullam quippe aliam melius hic intelligi puto columbam deargentatam, quam illam de qua

trilled with the divine word. The words of the Lord are elsewhere called purified silver, tried seven times with the fire of the earth. Certainly it is a great good to sleep in the midst of fortunes. Not a few took these fates for the two Testaments; so that sleeping in the midst of the lots is resting in the authority of the two Testaments, that is, assenting to the testimonies of both Testaments, so that, when something is uttered and proven by them, all controversy ends in peaceful calm. And if so, what else will appear to warn evangelizers with great power if not that then the Lord will give them the word so that they can evangelize if they sleep in the midst of the lots? For then the word of truth is given to them when they do not abandon the authority of both Testaments. Thus they will also be the silver wings of a dove, by whose preaching the glory of the Church will be carried to heaven. 18. On their backs. This is, indeed, a part of the body; part located near the region of the heart in the back, that is, on the back. This part of that silver dove is said to have the yellowness of gold, that is, the vigor of wisdom. I do not believe that anything better can be understood by this vigor than charity. But why does it have to be on the back and not on the chest? I can't explain how this word was written in another psalm, in which it is said: Between his back he will protect you and you will wait under his wings, since it cannot be covered under the wings if it were not covered by the chest. In Latin perhaps you can dictum est: Una est columba mea (Song 6,8). Deargentata est autem, quia divinis eloquiis est erudita: eloquia namque Domini alio loco dicuntur argentum igne examinedum terrae, purgatum septuplum (Ps 11,7). Magnum itaque aliquod bonum est, I will sleep Inter media cleros: quae nonnulli duo Testamenta esse voluerunt; ut dormite sit inter media cleros, in eorum Testamentum auctoritate requiescere; id est, utriusque Testamentí testimoniis acquiescere, ut qusndo aliquid ex his profertur et probatur, omnis contentio pacifica quiete finiatur. Quod si ita est, quid aliud admoneri videntur evangelizadores virtute Fine, nisi quia tune eis Dominus dabit verbum ut evangelizare possint, si dormiant Inter media cleros?

Tune enim eis verbum veritatis datur, si auctoritas ab eis duorum Testamentum non relinquatur: ut ipsi sint et pennae columbae deargentatae, quorum praedicatione in caelum gloria fertur Ecclesiae. 18. inter scapulas autem: pars est utique corporis; pars est circa regionem cordis, a posterioribus tamen, id est a verso: quam columbae illíus deargentatae partem in viridítate auri esse dicit, hoc est in vigore sapientiae; quem vigorem melius non puto intelligi posse quam charitatem. Sed quare a dorso, et non a pectore? Quanquam mirer quomodo positum sit hoc verbum in allio psalmo, ubi dicitur, inter scapulas suas obumbrabit tibi, et sub alis eius sperabis (Ps 90,4), cam sub alis obrumbrari non possit, nisi quod a pectore fuerit. Et latine quidem inter sca-

be understood inter scapulas (between the backs), in some way, by the anterior and posterior part, so that we take as the back what occupies the middle and main part of the body. In Hebrew it is perhaps doubtful that it can be understood in this way. But what is recorded in Greek metafrena only means "rear parts", that is, the backs. Is the yellowness of gold found there, that is, wisdom and charity, because there is, in a certain way, the origin of the wings or because the light load of the wings is supported there? However, what are the wings if not the two precepts of charity, in which all the law and the prophets are enclosed? And what is the light burden but charity itself, which is perfected or completed with these two precepts of love? What contains the precept of difficult or heavy, is light for the lover. For no other reason is it rightly understood that Christ said: My burden is light, but because he gives the Holy Spirit, by whom charity is diffused in our hearts, so that in loving we may do freely what he who acts servilely does with fear. He is not a friend of what is right who prefers, if possible, that what is just not be commanded. 19- Since it is not written: If you slept in the lots, but rather: In the middle of the lots, you can ask what it means in the middle of the lots. If this were translated more closely from Greek to Latin, it would be said inter médium clerorum and not inter -medios cleros (in the midst of the lots), which is not read in any Latin translator. That is why I believe that what was written is as valid: inter media cleros, as inter medium clerorum. Hence I will explain what I think. This word medium is usually adduced many times fortasse aliquo moda ex utraque parte possit intelligi, et ante, et post; ut scapulas accipiamus quae in medio caput habent: et in hebraeo sit fortassis ambiguum, quod possit et hoc moda intelligi; sed quod in graeco est UETácppEvcc, nonnisi a posterioribus significat, quod est inter scapulas. Utrum propterea ibi est auri viriditas, id est sapientia et charitas, quia ibi sunt quodammodo radices alarum; an quia ibi portatur illa sarcina levis? Quid enim sunt vel ipsae alae, nisi duo praecepta charitatis, in quibus tota Lex pendet et Prophetae? (Mt 22, 40).

Quid ipsa sarcina levis, nisi ipsa charitas quae in his duobus praeceptis impletur? Quidquid enim difficile est in praecepto, leve est amanti. In Greek it is doubtful whether the word "mountain" is in the nominative or accusative case, since in this language the word "mountain" is of the neuter gender and not of the masculine, as in Latin. And He also said: I will bring them back from Bashan. Basan means confusion. Then what does it mean that I will bring them back from confusion but that he who is ashamed or confused by his sins asks for God's mercy so that they may be remitted to him? This is why that publican did not dare to raise his eyes to heaven. Considering himself a sinner, he was ashamed, but he left the temple justified, because the Lord said: I will bring back Basan. Basan also means dryness or drought. And it is very well understood that the Lord brings back from dryness, that is, from destitution. For those who believe they are full, however, are hungry, and those who believe they are full, being empty, do not convert or return. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied. The Lord brings back from this dryness, since when the soul is thirsty, it is said: I stretched out my hands to you; My soul, like dry land, thirsts for you. The princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Neptali, As in the princes the apostles are symbolized, among whom is Benjamin, the youngest, in ecstasy, by whose words no one doubts that Saint Paul is pointed out; And since under the name of princes all the most outstanding and worthy of imitation are also designated in the churches, what do these names of the three tribes of Israel mean to indicate? If only Judah were mentioned, because the kings came from this tribe and from which our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh came from, we would think that the princes of the New Testament were also symbolized there; But since it is added: the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Neptali, perhaps someone will say that the apostles came from these and not from other tribes. However, since I also do not find how it can be refuted and furthermore in this place I note that the princes of the churches and the leaders of those who bless the Lord in the churches are recommended, I also accept this opinion with reason; but I confess that I like much more what is implied by the meaning of these names. These names are Hebrew names that mean: Judah, confession; Zebulun, abode of strength, and Neptalí, my extension. Well, the first thing that occurs in martyrdom is confession, and in favor of it one receives the strength to endure everything that happens; and after having suffered everything, the work is over, the extension of the prize is achieved. It can also be understood, given the case, that the Apostle mainly recommends the following three virtues: faith, hope and charity, which are represented: in faith, confession; in hope, strength, and in charity, extension or prolongation, since it is characteristic of faith "that it is created with the heart for righteousness and with the mouth it is confessed for health"; of hope, strengthening in sadness, which brings with it the tribulation coming from suffering: if we hope for what we do not see, we wait patiently; of charity, diffusion or prolongation, well, it is in itself diffusive; and also because perfect charity casts out fear, which brings with it the torment due to the anguish or narrowness of the soul. Then the princes of Judah, their leaders, who bless the Lord in the churches, and the princes of Zebulun, and the princes of Neptali, who are princes of confession, of strength and of extension or prolongation, are the princes of faith, hope and charity. 37 [v.29]. Oh God, command your strength. This is our only Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made, and we for Him, for of Him we read that He is the strength and wisdom of God. But how does God send his Christ if not by enhancing him? God enhances his own charity in us because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us and gave us all things with Him. Send, O God, to your strength; consolidate, oh confessio est, et pro illa quidquid acciderit tolerandi sequens assumitur fortitudo; deinde post omnia tolerata, finitis angustiis, latitudo consequitur in praemio. Potest et sic intelligi, ut quoniam tria haec praecipue commendat Apostolus, fidem, spem, charitatem (2 Cor 13:13), confessio sit in fide, fortitudo in spe, latitudo in charitate. Fidei quippe res est ut corde credatur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fiat ad salutem (Rom 10,10). In passionibus autem tribulationum res tristis est, sed spes fortis est: Si enim quod non videmus speramus, per patientiam exspectamus (Ib. 8,25). Latitudinem vero praestat charitatis in corde diffusio: nam consummata charitas joras mittit timorem (1 lo 4,18); qui timor tormentum habet per animae anguishes.

Many Latin codices, and especially the Greek ones, arrange these verses in such a way that in them there is not one and the same verse that says for God the kingdoms of the earth, but they place the word Deo (for God) at the end of the previous verse, and thus say: Aethiopia praeveniet manus eius Deo, and then another verse follows, saying: Regna terrae, cantate Deo, psallite Domino (Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God, praise the Lord). Since this division exists, which is based on the authority of many codices and on conformity with the most worthy ones, it seems to me that the one that puts faith before works should be recommended and preferred, because the wicked is justified by faith without the merits of good works, as the Apostle says: To him who believes in Him who justifies the wicked, righteousness is imputed to him, so that later faith begins to work through love, since only good works should be called good works. that are executed by the charity of God. It is necessary that this faith precedes, so that through it and not through them (the others) it begins, that is, charity, since no one works for the charity of God if he does not first believe in God. From Ethiopia itself, since in the Greek text it is not obscure, since the word autes (eius, hers or hers) is written in the feminine gender. In justifying himself, he does not boast of the works of the law nor does he put his merits before faith, but rather he anticipates his faith before his works. The title of the psalm is the following: For the end; in

favor of those who are to be changed; for David. Understand that this change must be something better. The change can be made for better or worse. That of Adam and Eve became worse. Those who, coming from Adam and Eve, were united to Christ were changed into something better. For as through a man death (came), so through a man the resurrection of the dead (took place); and as in Adam all die, so all are made alive in Christ. What God formed, Adam changed, but into something worse, because of his iniquity. What iniquity wrought, believers change, but into something better, through the grace of God. Our change into something worse was due to our iniquity. Changing into something better is not done by our justice, but by the grace of God. Then let us blame ourselves for having been changed into something worse; To be better is the glory of God. This psalm (speaks) in favor of those who are to be changed. And where does this change come from if it is not from the passion of Christ? The word pascha (Easter) is translated into Latin by transitus (step). It is not a Greek name, but a Hebrew one. In the Greek language it sounds like passion, because suffering is written pasjein, but, examining the Hebrew word pascha, it means something else. Easter remembers the passage or transit. This was warned by the evangelist Saint John, who, before the imminence of the passion, when the Lord celebrated the dinner in which he gave the sacrament of his body and blood, says: The hour having arrived in which Jesus was to pass from this world to the Father. Then he expressed the transit of passion. If he who came for us had not passed from here to the Father, how could we have passed from here?

Quod admonuit etiam Ioannes evangelista, qui imminente passione, cum vinoret Dominus ad coenam qua commendavit sacramentum corporis et sanguinis sui, ita loquitur: Cum autem venisset hora, qua transiret Iesus de hoc mundo ad Patrem (lo 13,1). Expressit ergo transitum Paschae. Sed nisi ipse transiret hinc ad Patrem, qui propter nos venit, nos trasiré

here, that we have not descended to lift something, but that we have fallen? But He did not fall, but came down to lift up the one who had fallen. Then it is about his transit and ours: from here, to the Father; from this world, to the kingdom of heaven; from this mortal life, to the eternal; from earthly life to heavenly life; from corruptible life to incorruptible life; from the familiarity of tribulations, to perpetual security. That is why the title of the psalm is in favor of those who are to be changed. Then let us notice in the text of the psalm the reason for our change, that is, the passion of the Lord, and our voice in the midst of tribulations; let us recognize it, we groan. And so, hearing, knowing and groaning, let us be changed, so that the title of the psalm may be fulfilled in us: In favor of those who are to be changed. 3 [v. 2]. Save me, O God! -because the waters have penetrated to my soul. Now that mustard seed is despised, because it seems to cry out with a patient voice. To be born it is buried; Later the world will admire the magnitude of the plant, whose seed the Jews mocked. In fact, consider that the mustard seed is very small, dark, contemptible; Thus what was said is fulfilled here: We saw him, and he had no form or beauty. He says that the waters have penetrated to his soul because those mobs, which he designated by the man of water, increased their power in such a way that they killed Christ. They prevailed to the point of despising him, arresting him, tying him up, insulting him, slapping him, spitting on him... Until what else? Until I kill him. Then the waters have penetrated hinc quomodo possemus, qui non propter aliquid levandum descendimus, sed cecidimus? Ipse autem non cecidit; sed descendit, ut eum qui ceciderat sublevaret. Transitus ergo, et illius, et noster, hinc ad Patrem; from hoc mundo ad regnum caelorum, from vita mortali ad vitam aeternam, from vita terrena ad vitam caelestem, from vita corruptibili ad incorruptibilem, from tribulationum conversatione ad perpetuara securitatem. Ideo, Pro his qui commutabuntw; Psalmi titulus est. Causam igitur commutationis nostrae, id est ipsam Domini passionem, nostramque in tribulationibus vocem in textu Psalmi advertamus, cognoscamus, congemiscamus: et audiendo, cognoscendo, congemiscendo, mutemur, ut impleatur in nobis titulus Psalmi, Pro his qui commutabuntur. 3 [v.2].

Salvum me fac, Deus, quoniam introierunt aquae usque ad animam meam. Granum illud est contemptum moda, quod videtur humiles I will cry out. In horto obruitur, miraturo mundo oleris magnitudeinem, cuius oleris semen contemptum est a Iudaeis. Revera enim consider semen sinapis minutum, fuscum, aspernabile prorsus; ut ibi impleatur quod dictum est: Vidimus eum, et no» habebat speciem ñeque decorem (Is 53,2). Aquas autem intrasse usque ad animam suam dicit; quia potuerunt illae turbae, quas aquarum nomine significavit, huc usque praevalere, ut occiderent Christum. Praevaluerunt ad contemnendum, ad tenendum, ad ligandum, ad insultandum, ad colaphizandum, ad conspuendum. Adhuc quousque? Usque ad mortem. Ergo introierunt aquae usque ad animam meam. Hanc quippe vitam dixit animam suam, quousque
Prayer of the vexed people

even my soul. He called this life a soul, to which they could, by being cruel, approach. But could they have achieved it if He had not allowed it? Then how does he cry out in this way, appearing to endure something against his own will, if it is not because the head symbolizes his members? He suffered because he wanted to; On the contrary, martyrs suffer without wanting it. This is how he predicted his passion to Saint Peter: When you become old, another will gird you and take you where you do not want to go. As much as we long to be united with Christ, yet we do not want to die; and for this we willingly or, rather, patiently suffer, since there is no other way to adhere to Christ. If we could reach Christ by another way, that is, to eternal life, who would want to die? The apostle Saint Paul, explaining in a certain place our nature, that is, the union of soul and body, and the intimacy and connection of this union, says that we have a house not made with hands, eternal in heaven; that is, an immortality prepared for us, with which we must clothe ourselves at the end, when we rise from the dead; And he adds that those of us who are in this current nature do not want to undress, but rather overdress, so that what is mortal is absorbed by life. If it could happen, he says, we would want to become immortal, so that, arriving at immortality being what we are, it would change us, so that this mortal of ours would be absorbed by life without passing the body through death, thus finally taking on the second garment. Although we currently pass from evils to good, however, this transition is somewhat bitter and has the gall that the Jews gave the Lord to drink in the passion; and has also illi accessé saeviendo potuerunt. Sed numquid hoc possent, nisi ab ipso permitterentur? Unde ergo tanquam aliquid invitus patiatur sic clamat, nisi quia caput membra sua praefigurat? Passus est quippe ille, quia voluit; martyres vero, etiamsi noluerunt. Petro namque ita praedixit passionem suam: Cum senueris, inquit, alius te praecinget, et feret quo tu non vis (lo 21,18). Quanquam enim Christo inhaerere cupiamus, mori tamen nolumus; et ideo libenfer, vel potíus patienter patimur, quia alius transitus non datur, per quem Christo cohaereamus.

Nam si possemus aliter pervenire ad Christum, id est ad vitam aeternam, quis vellet mori? Naturam quippe nostram, id est consortium quoddam animae et corporis; et quamdam in his duobus familiaritatem conglutinationis atque compaginis exposens quodam loco Apostolus, ait habere nos domum non manufactam, aeternam in caelis; id est immortalitatem praeparatam nobis, qua induendi sumus in fine, cum resurrexerimus a mortuis; et ait: In quo nolumus spoliari, sed supervestiri, ut absorbatur moríale a vita (2 Cor 5,1.4). Si fieri posset, sic vellemus, ait, fieri immortales, ut iam vinoet ipsa immortalitas, et moda sicut sumus mutaret nos, ut mortale hoc nostrum a vita absorbetur, non per mortem Corpusponeretur, ut in fine iterum reciperetur. Quamvis ergo a malis ad bona transeamus; tamen ipse transitus aliquantum amarus est, et habet fel, quod dederunt Domino in passione Iudaei, habet acre quiddam toleraten-
